speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pertaining to the apparent serious mistreatment of the chief steward, a government employee for ten years under two Prime Ministers, at the Prime Minister's official residence, 24 Sussex Drive.
I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Marquette:
That the Prime Minister make a statement as to why the position held by Mr. Tom MacDonald, Chief Steward at 24 Sussex Drive for ten years, has been suddenly declared bilingual when all those in the household speak English; whether Mr. MacDonald is being forced to terminate his employment in the spring and what specific part, if any, was played by the Prime Minister's wife in this regrettable and unnecessary designation of a bilingual position.

subtopic: PROPOSED LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR SUPERVISED SECRET STRIKE BALLOT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I wonder then, if the minister would indicate if at this initiative he is going to put this before the tripartite body.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a question for the Minister of Finance. Further to his earlier
9630

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-APPLICABILITY OF GUIDELINES TO PRICE OF NATURAL GAS
speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice arising out of the unanimous decision of the Supreme Court of Canada written by the Chief Justice and involving the former chairman of the anti-dumping tribunal. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION ON MISUSE OF CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION-INSTRUCTIONS TO LAW OFFICERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I read the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada with a good deal of concern and I appreciate the hon. member raising the question. I have asked for a full report of the circumstances surrounding the case, which occurred some years ago. I have not received a report because of the absence of one of my counsel in Toronto. I want to assure the hon. member however, and the House, that I do not condone, and have so indicated to my officers, the use of either the Income Tax Act or the Combines Investigation Act except for the purposes spelled out in those acts. I want to make it very clear that I have put this position to my officials. I am determining the factors surrounding that case and I feel fairly sure that neither of my two immediate predecessors have condoned the use of material obtained under those Acts for purposes not provided for in the Acts.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the document I have just tabled, "The Final Act of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe"-called from the outset by its initials CSCE-was signed at Helsinki on August 1 by the heads of government of the states of Europe and of Canada and the United States. It is intended to establish the basis for the development of future relations between their countries and peoples. It is, therefore, an entirely forwardlooking document; it does not look back to the past.
Many Canadians have been erroneously led to believe that by signing the Final Act of the CSCE Canada and its allies did something that sanctified the status quo in Europe. It is true that the Soviet Union for the last thirty years and during the course of the CSCE itself sought to gain acceptance of the political and geographical situation in Europe. But throughout the conference the NATO allies worked to avoid a document that could be pointed to in years to come as a surrogate peace treaty for World War II. Not one word of the Final Act justifies the claim that it constitutes recognition of Soviet hegemony in eastern Europe or of the post-war de facto borders.
Canada entered the negotiations with a specific set of concerns. We wanted to play a part in the conference commensurate with our interests in Europe. In this we succeeded. We wanted to see incorporated in the Final Act measures to assist the freer movement of people and ideas. This goal has been achieved. Worthy of special note in this regard is the strong text on the reunification of families, sponsored by Canada.
December 2, 1975

We sought the development of a confidence-building measure involving advance notification of military manoeuvres, and after difficult negotiations such a measure was worked out. Finally, Canada had important economic and environmental interests to safeguard and advance, and the appropriate texts in the Final Act meet our requirements in this respect.
The Final Act provides for a meeting at senior official level in Belgrade in 1977 to review progress in implementation and possibly to organize a resumed conference. It is the policy of the government to ensure that, for its part, the Final Act is implemented as soon and as completely as possible. Copies are being sent to all federal government departments and agencies concerned, to provincial governments and to non-governmental organizations whose cooperation is essential to the carrying out of Canada's responsibilities under the Final Act. Copies are now available to the public through the outlets of Information Canada.
Domestically, we are examining what changes should be made in our present practices to meet the moral commitments we have accepted. In our bilateral relations we are using the document to provide guidance in communiques, agreements and treaties. Multilaterally, consideration is already being given to the matter of implementation in two United Nations bodies, the Economic Commission for Europe, and UNESCO.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one would never accuse the Department of External Affairs of acting in haste. The document tabled in the House today, the Final Act signed in Helsinki on August 1, 1975, was published in the September issue of "International Legal Materials" and has been reposing since then in the Library of Parliament, where I first read it. This raises the interesting question of what other documentation the government has consigned to the library shelves rather than bringing it into the House for the inspection of parliament. One thinks immediately of the "New International Economic Order," a document that has occupied the attention of two special sessions of the United Nations General Assembly, which has yet to receive the official notice or attention of parliament.
In the case of the Final Act of Helsinki, the reason for the delay may be found in the distinct discomfiture evidenced in the minister's statement; for however much the minister may claim that the Final Act does not justify Soviet control over eastern Europe, this is precisely the effect. We are to go forward, the minister says, not dwell on the past. Are we to forget the millions of east Europeans trampled on in the Soviet Union's unprincipled expansion? Are we to forget the dead, the tortured, the prison camps, the ceaseless violations of human rights by a totalitarian regime that seeks to legitimize its actions through the floss of detente?
What in fact has happened-the Canadian people should be aware of this-is that the Final Act gives the Kremlin its long-sought symbolic hegemony over eastern Europe in trade for unenforceable, limp pledges for an increased east-west flow of information, ideas and people. Brezhnev himself claimed that Helsinki was "a necessary summing-
European Security
up of the political outcome of the Second World War". In effect, the signatures of 35 nations have recognized the status quo in eastern and central Europe established by Russian arms in the interest of Russian power. Let us not hide the fact that Helsinki was a betrayal of the victims of oppression.
The question we must now ask is; Are we betraying ourselves in putting hope in this document which has no legally binding effect? The Helsinki principles oblige the signatories to support liberty of thought, conscience and faith, the exercise of civil and political rights, a freer flow of information, ideas and people, in addition to basic principles of relations between states; non-intervention, sovereign equality, self-determination, territorial integrity, inviolability of frontiers. All of this is the stuff of security and co-operation, but not one of these principles is being honoured today by the Soviet Union.
It takes heroic willpower to read the Final Act without giving in to cynicism. What could better demonstrate the bad faith of the Soviet Union than the refusal to allow Soviet physicist Andrei Sakharov to go to Oslo to receive his Nobel Peace Prize on December 10?

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
This refusal is an affront to world public opinion; and Sakharov is right when he says that this refusal confirms the continued Soviet violation of human rights which imperils the future of all mankind. Our party will begin to believe Helsinki when we see Sakharov in Oslo, when we see unrestricted movement of Soviet Jews, when we see the Polish people, the Czechoslovaks, the Ukrainians and other subjugated east Europeans living the life of their choice. Only then talk to us about reducing Canada's military commitments in Europe-not before.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, our party is pleased to see the sections on the reunification of families that Canada insisted be in the Final Act. The Act states that "participating states will deal in a positive and humanitarian spirit with the applications of persons who wish to be reunited with members of their family". Why, then, are four former Rumanian citizens, David Pompiliu of Toronto, Dimitrie Moldovan of Edmonton, Julian Hirtescu of Toronto, and Alexandre Sandu of Quebec City, ignored by the government as they stand outside the parliament buildings day by day in peaceful pleading that Canada help to reunite their families detained in Rumania? I have brought these four men into the House today as my guests and we are asking for action from the government.
Helsinki could open the way to a really serious western commitment to economic and social justice for the developing nations of the Third World. That would be the greatest of all foundations for the global peace we desire. But in the meantime, let us not delude ourselves. The more we study Helsinki's Final Act, the more we understand the minister's reluctance to bring it into the House.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House knows that the purpose of the conference was to promote security in Europe through detente. The Final Act of the conference deals with some military matters, such as notification of manoeuvres, but recognizes the truth that security does not depend upon the piling up of armaments

December 2, 1975
European Security
but on the good will, the understanding and the co-operation of the peoples concerned. Indeed, the piling up of armaments to existing levels, not least by the two superpowers, is a perpetual source of insecurity.
This Final Act expresses many highly desirable aspirations in a variety of fields and throughout 132 pages. But the proof of the pudding will be in the eating. The real question will be the implementation of all these noble words. The Act speaks of sovereignty and equality of states, of the territorial integrity of states, the inviolability of frontiers, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and refraining from the threat or use of force. In his statement, the minister was at pains to say that there is nothing in the document that sanctifies the status quo in Europe. That may be technically correct, but in reality there can be little doubt that the document clearly rejects the use of force to alter presently existing boundaries. I do not complain of that. In what he said, I do not know whether the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) was suggesting that we should not accept this treaty because we had some other alternative to changing the boundaries of eastern Europe. As far as we are concerned, we think that in the nuclear age talk of using force to alter the boundaries of eastern Europe makes no sense at all.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: He didn't say that.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
The document goes on to make promises in respect of human rights and freedom. These high-sounding sentiments have been used frequently in this era in many parts of the world, not only in eastern Europe, but the abuse of human rights and fundamental freedom in many parts of the world remains a grim reality. There are provisions for co-operation in very many fields. If these proposals for co-operation in fact are taken up and implemented, perhaps we will have a different atmosphere.
As has been pointed out, there is provision for the reunification of families and of regular meetings on the basis of family ties. Once again, it is the implementation, not the announcement of these humanitarian measures, that is required. The good intentions of the European nations on both sides of the iron curtain are clearly and, indeed, eloquently expressed in the document. I think that is to the good, but it will take a lot of hard work and good will on both sides to remove the fears and suspicions that years of hostility have built up.
Canada should be glad to be associated in this important task, even if we may be skeptical about some of the phases through which this treaty is bound to go before it is fully implemented. We can be skeptical, but let us not reject the means made available, through the treaty, to the peoples of Europe, with the co-operation of North America, of building a sounder, more stable world.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in principle everybody favours peace and co-operation between nations, but we must come to see, through the show given by heads in Helsinki, the realities and consequences. In my opinion, a treaty such as this offers no real safeguard. Mere signatures at the bottom of a formal document are not enough to guarantee peace and security. Past experiences

bearing this, the 1939 pact between Molotov and von Rib-bentrop, as well as the treaty between Hitler and Chamberlain, are bitter mementos which warn us never to forget this reality. Western countries, led by the United States, have renounced their true roles to concentrate their efforts on the search for gains and profits, even to the point of providing all components for nuclear world war.
On one hand, peace is advocated in very many speeches, as Mr. Ford was doing in China yesterday and on the other hand we make and sell as many weapons as we can while believing that they will never be used! Meanwhile, the U.S.S.R. is acting along the same line in its own way: they are advocating detente, making believe it is peace, while continuing just as before to extend their hold country by country, continent by continent. Just see what is going on in Portugal at the very moment I am speaking. Nobody has spoken about the bursting in Portugal where the "Russian detente" is becoming apparent nor about the divisions in Cyprus, nor about the arms race, nor about the West Berlin status.
The Helsinki Act, signed by more than 35 countries- including the United States with Canada "in their pocket"-represents the official recognition of the U.S.S.R. right to absolute property over the lands conquered during World War II and over the countries which, thereafter, have been maintained by force within the soviet system.
It represents the doom of the East European countries without any hope of freedom for the future. It is an alarm for China, confronted by the increasing Soviet threat, as the Chinese authorities emphasized again yesterday in Peking. The Helsinki pact gives Russia absolute liberty to do what she wants and to extend her hegemony without anybody saying a word, for fear of being called an enemy of detente.
The Helsinki agreement is an acknowledgement of the weakening of western countries and America, through the multiplication of compromises and concessions. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) pointed out, at the beginning of his speech, that the countries had "not to look back to the past" to reach this agreement. If we look at what this agreement really brought to us, our countries must have really forgotten everything that has happened to reach it. I hope nonetheless that they will not awake too late or too suddenly. We also hope that the next meeting of ministers of external affairs, which is to be held, according to the minister, in 1977, will be a source of more optimism about the future of the whole world for all nations.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief question for the minister as a result of the statement he made today. On Friday, November 28, I mentioned that Rumanian citizens who now have landed immigrant status in Canada were parading in front of the parliament buildings seeking Canadian government assistance in bringing their families to Canada. The minister promised to follow up my request in order to obtain the reunification of these families in accordance with the agreement reached at the Helsinki conference. I ask the minister what steps have been taken by him and his officials with regard to this request, and what response, if any, has been received from the Rumanian embassy?
December 2, 1975

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a matter of course we are constantly in touch with the embassies and officials of governments such as Rumania to accelerate the process of reunification of families from eastern Europe under the terms of the Helsinki agreement. I have not at the present time a specific report on each of these cases, but I will be in touch with my hon. friend later. While I am on the subject of family reunification, may I say that Canada regards the implementation of the final act, particularly in respect of family reunification, as a measure of the true attitude of participants in the conference. Because the deputy minister of the foreign office of Hungary is in the gallery, I should mention that we are pleased to note that all the active family reunification cases which were included on the list given to Hungarian officials earlier this year appear to have been successfully resolved.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a couple of questions to the minister. He has said, on one hand, that this is not a binding treaty and, therefore, there is no legal recognition of the boundaries that came into force following World War II-obtained, of course, by force. He has said, on the other hand, that there is a moral commitment in respect of family reunification. It seems to me the minister is trying to have it both ways in regard to this treaty. Either it has a legal and binding effect, or it does not. Either it offers real hope for family reunification, or it does not. I should like the minister to explain the effect of the treaty other than to give respectability to detente.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
On the first point, Mr. Speaker, I think it has to be made clear that the results of the conference do not, notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman has stated, endorse the territorial status quo in Europe. That was not the result of the conference and we worked very hard to avoid that outcome. The text recognizes that while existing boundaries in Europe are inviolable, and indeed they continue to be, they can be changed in accordance with international law by peaceful means or agreement. I believe the more we repeat the erroneous statement that the status quo was sanctified by this conference, the easier we will make it for certain people to draw that conclusion-a conclusion that is not supported and is contrary to the words of the text. My hon. friend ought to be conscious of that possibility which would be very damaging to the cause that he is ostensibly supporting.
The document is not a legal document. It is a statement of principle. It is not a treaty. It does not have legal effect. All the countries have come together in accepting these principles, one of which is the principle of the acceleration of family reunification. Of course, we intend to insist-as this House is insisting today-that all signatories live up to and implement these principles. When we come to the monitoring conference in Belgrade in 1977 we will know to what extent the signatories have lived up to the principles to which they put their signature at Helsinki. That is the significance of the document: it is a standard against which the performance of the signatories can be measured. That is a very important result.
European Security

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is precisely because the Helsinki Final Act is a statement of principle that we wish to have clarified the whole question of the family reunification clause. I ask the minister now, how can we expect people to believe in the Helsinki Final Act if we do not see very quick action on the reunification of families?
In addition to the question of Hungary that he has volunteered, we are bringing to this country representatives of Rumania, people who have left that country and have had two or three years without their families and whose case has been brought to the attention of the Canadian government. The Canadian government granted entrance visas for their families, but it is the exit visas from Rumania which are not being issued and which the Canadian government has not yet protested.
I ask the minister now if he will assure the House this afternoon, in the presence of the four Rumanians I have mentioned that a personal protest will be carried by the Department of External Affairs to the government of Rumania on their behalf.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: With the greatest respect, the question bears great similarity to that put by the hon. members colleague, the member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), which was answered by the minister in a manner which would indicate that he does not have the details of those cases in front of him, but that he will deal with them later. Therefore, I do not think I can permit the second question.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister. I have to agree with my colleagues here, but there is one specific question. In order to maintain a more speedy flow of visas for the reunification of families between Russia and Canada according to the Helsinki accords, will the minister ask his department to set up consular offices in Leningrad and Kiev and ask the Russians to do the same? There are those other than Muscovites who want to be reunited with their families; for example, there are many Ukrainian families in Kiev and Leningrad.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
The purpose of the text on family reunification was to alter and to improve the existing practice. It is my view that it is too early to condemn the Helsinki document on non-performance at this stage. Maybe we must do that later on, but I believe we must now insist that all signatories live up to the principle which states that participating states will deal in a positive and humanitarian way with the applications of persons who wish to be reunited with members of their family. That is the principle, and we will insist on its implementation in the course of our discussions with representatives of other countries. In my discussion with Mr. Gromyko just recently, this was one of the points I made with him.
With regard to opening up new posts in parts of the Soviet Union for purposes which are entirely commendable, I am afraid I cannot hold out any hope that in this period of restraint it will be possible for my department to increase its posts in any country.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all it would require would be one individual in each of these cities in order to expedite the visas. According to the Helsinki principles, would the minister advise the Russian government to stop charging excess duty-this is part and parcel of the Helsinki accord
9638

December 2, 1975
European Security
and the Helsinki principles-on parcels which are sent from Canada to families in the Soviet Union, including items such as foodstuffs and clothing. I think this is wrong according to the Helsinki principles.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this particular question is a new one for me. I must say there are other principles in the document, but one, of course, is the principle of sovereignty. All these principles have to operate together. While each country has undertaken to live up to these principles, they all have to be taken in their total context. However, I should like to examine the details of the question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Order, please. I would propose, in the circumstances, to conclude the questioning by recognizing the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin), and the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek).

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to reiterate, again, my thanks for the efforts of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), especially in the field of family reunification. However, on the question of peace I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he is prepared this afternoon to inform the House whether any progress has been made at the conference in Geneva, at which Canada is a participant, relating to the Mutual and Balanced Force Reductions in central and eastern Europe.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Regretfully, Mr. Speaker, I must inform the House and my hon. friend that no progress has been made up to the present time in the discussions on the MBFR. I have made clear, I believe all hon. members will agree, that if the process of detente is to be meaningful it must be accompanied by progress in respect of the reduction of arms in Europe. That has not yet taken place. At the NATO meeting which I will be attending next week that subject will be a matter for discussion by the members of the alliance.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister seems to have great confidence in the document he tabled this afternoon, which is, after a fashion, a statement of principle.
How can he explain, for instance, with regard to the free exchange of information between the countries mentioned in the document, that at the time of the conference Mr. Brezhnev indicated that exchanges would be free provided there was an agreement on their extent, which really means, to all practical purposes, that the Russians reserve the right to do what they have always done in that regard?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON "THE FINAL ACT OF THE CONFERENCE ON SECURITY AND CO-OPERATION IN EUROPE"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find no ready answer to the statement which the hon. member has made, except to repeat that now the principles have been accepted, we have to continue to insist that they be implemented and, at the time we are all together at a meeting in Belgrade, tell each other what we think of the performance or lack of performance. That will likely be the test of the words and principles which have been adopted.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, December 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-73, to provide for the restraint of profit margins, prices, dividends and compensation in Canada, be read the third time and do pass.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I began my remarks yesterday in connection with this bill I indicated, as I have on other occasions, that members of this party in parliament have said from the beginning that a program of wage and price controls, as it has been recently called, would inevitably be doomed to failure because we are faced with an international problem which cannot be dealt with by one country alone.
I indicated, also, that it was obvious to us from everything that has happened since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave notice of the introduction of this policy on Thanksgiving day, from the statements made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) publicly, from the statements made by the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, and from the discussions which have been held between representatives of the provinces and the federal government, that even if we had believed, as the Premier of Manitoba believed, that an incomes policy that was fair and equitable to all people of Canada was necessary and workable to dampen the ill effects of inflation, in fact we are not going to get that.
After I have discussed some of the statements, and the failure to make statements, by the chairman of the AntiInflation Board, I want to put on the record some of the detailed questions put to the Minister of Finance and to the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board a week ago, at a meeting of the ministers of finance, by the Premier of Manitoba-questions which, I am told by senior members of the Manitoba delegation, were not answered at all by the Minister of Finance or by the chairman of the AntiInflation Board. Such was the situation that the Premier of Manitoba, who was a proponent of an incomes policy when the Prime Minister was still opposing wage and price controls, indicated pretty clearly that he has no expectation that the program proposed by the federal government has any hope of success. I will come back to that point shortly, but first I want to deal with the actions and inactions of the so called Anti-Inflation Board.
In the guidelines issued by the Minister of Finance on October 14, 1975, entitled "Attack on Inflation", on page 23-where compensation and exceptions to the 10 per cent

limit in the increase which will be permitted in wages and salaries are dealt with-the minister said:
There may also be other grounds lor exceptions, such as increases necessary to maintain long-established historical relationships between wages in closely related groups and other special cases of equity.
Today, the postal workers represented by the Canadian Union of Postal Workers have agreed to go back to work after a seven weeks' strike. They have agreed to go back on the basis of an offer by the federal government which is substantially more than the 10 per cent which is supposedly the limit which any group of workers earning wages or salaries can get. Why will they be permitted to get an increase of more than 10 per cent? According to the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), who certainly is no friend of the postal workers or of their union, they will get an increase of more than 10 per cent because there has been a historical relationship; there has been parity for years between the inside postal workers represented by CUPW and the outside workers represented by the Letter Carriers Union.
Let us look at what is happening to the teachers in Toronto. I have already indicated what the minister supposedly thought and meant when he issued his guidelines. The chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board said on November 8 that it was not the intention of the board to replace the collective bargaining process. He said it was expected that the parties would negotiate in good faith with a view to concluding agreements under the guidelines. Then he indicated that after agreement had been reached, if the agreement was for more than the 10 per cent indicated as a limit under the guidelines, the employer and the union could come to the Anti-Inflation Board and argue that they should be permitted to get more than 10 per cent. But the Anti-Inflation Board, supposedly, was not going to interfere in the regular process of free, collective bargaining.
Now what do we find? We find that under the provisions of the legislation enacted by the Ontario government, a fact-finder was appointed to look into the dispute between the Toronto secondary school teachers and their employer, the board of education. That fact-finder made a series of recommendations substantially higher than the guidelines would permit. Those recommendations were accepted by the Toronto teachers' organization. The board of education rejected them. It was willing to settle for the same amount as it had already settled for with the elementary school teachers, a settlement reached before the Prime Minister announced his policy, agreed to by both sides and implemented. The board of education wanted to settle with the secondary school teachers for the same amount and the same conditions they had reached with the elementary school teachers. That has been the pattern in the city of Toronto for 21 years.
However, we have an anti-inflation policy. We have supposed guidelines, so the Toronto board of education did what the Anti-Inflation Board had said it would not permit. It appealed to the Anti-Inflation Board, unilaterally, to look at the problem and to issue a directive. What do we find? Just a few weeks after the chairman said that the board would not disturb the traditional ways of collective bargaining and would not deal with one side of an argument, the Anti-Inflation Board issues a directive. I quote
December 2, 1975

from the Globe and Mail of Saturday, November 29, as follows:
"The latest offer of the metro Toronto school board to its secondary teachers is in excess of the amount which the Anti-Inflation Board would consider appropriate", Jean-Luc Pepin, chairman of the federal agency, told reporters. Teachers and school trustees should "return to the bargaining table in an effort to reach an agreement that more properly reflects the anti-inflation policy of restraint"-
How many times will they have to return to the bargaining table? If the offer is reduced by 5 per cent, will that be acceptable to the chairman?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: We don't know.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The chairman is now God; he does not have to account to anyone but himself. The school board made its offer to keep secondary school salaries in line with the increase accepted by elementary school teachers before the guidelines were brought in, but obviously the historical and traditional patterns are going to be ignored. So we have a situation where elementary school teachers are to be paid more than secondary school teachers. Metro public school teachers received a raise of 39.2 per cent, the same percentage offered to the high school teachers, but the metro school board seems now to be barred by the federal guidelines.
The minister refuses to do anything about it, although the Ontario Secondary School Teachers Federation has supplied to the Anti-Inflation Board and to the minister a list of 12 regions which are already paying higher salaries than the Toronto board of education has offered: these are Windsor, Ottawa, Carleton, Halton, Nipissing, York region, Simcoe, Manitoulin, Huron, North Shore, Grey and Thunder Bay. Is it any wonder that the Toronto schools teachers said the Minister of Finance had lied to them? I am not surprised. What we have is a board which has violated and ignored the guidelines laid down by the minister, and it is being aided and abetted by the minister in ignoring them.
I said that I would put on the record some of the questions the province of Manitoba asked the minister and the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board last week. I wish to begin with one set of questions which are very pertinent. Today's Globe and Mail has a story which is headed-I will go into some detail on this-"Bank balances of revenue show impressive increases." The chairman of the AntiInflation Board, who was so quick to ignore the salary guidelines and so quick to reject what he said two weeks ago namely, that he would not intervene on one side or the other and would only make a ruling after both sides in a dispute had come to an agreement, has been conspicuous by his silence.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
It is not as if he did not know about this until today. Here are some of the questions asked a week ago of the Minister of Finance and the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board by the Premier of Manitoba who, as I indicated earlier, was and is a strong proponent of a real incomes policy:
Bank profits have continued to increase rapidly this year-the Financial Times is predicting industry-wide gains of 30 per cent for the current year-with further increases in sight. Yet the federal government seems to suggest that banks should continue operating exactly as they are. Two questions:
Anti-Inflation Act
(a)	Has the federal government given any thought to requiring banks to reduce the margin between the interest rates they charge on loans and the interest rates they pay on deposits?
(b)	Has the federal government given any consideration to requiring banks and other financial institutions to set aside more substantial funds for housing and other socially desirable activity?
The Minister of Finance is here and he can correct me if I am misrepresenting what happened, but I am told by senior members of the Manitoba delegation that they asked questions and received no answers from the minister, and just the usual, silly grin which we have seen almost every day on television from the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I will be surprised if within six months of ending his tenure as chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, the "honourable"-I put that in quotation marks-Jean-Luc Pepin is not a director of one of the largest banks in Canada.
Why was the government of Manitoba so concerned? Let us look at the figures released today by the banks themselves and reported in the Globe and Mail. Let us look at the operating profit, after tax, for the year 1975 over the year 1974. For the Royal Bank of Canada, 126.6 per cent; for the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, 58.4 per cent; for the Bank of Montreal, 148.6 per cent; for the Bank of Nova Scotia, 80.5 per cent; for the Toronto-Dominion Bank, 58.6 per cent; for the Provincial Bank, 71 per cent; for the Mercantile Bank, 149.3 per cent.
It is not my job as a Member of Parliament to defend or to criticize, for example, the postal workers, but the Postmaster General and the Government of Canada forced them into a seven-week strike because they asked for more than 29 per cent over 30 months. Yet here are the banks making a 40 per cent to 150 per cent higher profit, and not a word from the Minister of Finance.
Does this minister expect that when it is so obvious there is to be no equity in this program, workers will accept it quietly? Does he expect that there will be peace in this country? Does he expect that what has happened to productivity-that is, a lowering of productivity, which all the economists and business leaders have been bemoaning- will not continue and will not accelerate? Does he expect that workers will really work when they feel, and correctly so, that they are being hard done by and discriminated against? There is no question in my mind that some postal workers will not feel like working very hard. Teachers in Toronto have already announced that they will work to rule. That means there will be virtually no athletic programs, virtually no dramatic programs, and that exam papers will not be marked on weekends; and if people have to wait for the reports, that will just be too bad.
The railway unions are about to negotiate. If the companies, on the suggestion or the direction of the government, insist on a 10 per cent limit on wage increases, despite the sound principles laid down by Mr. Justice Hall two or three years ago on how demands for wage increases should be dealt with, there is no doubt that a large number of railway workers will decide to work to rule if they cannot

Anti-Inflation Act
have what they think they are entitled to. The resultant slowdown in the day to day operations of the railways will be brought about by the thinking of the minister and the government.
Let us look at some important questions asked by the government of Manitoba which the minister has refused to answer. Of course, he cannot answer them because he never intended to do anything about incomes, except on wages and salaries. He never intended to do anything about prices, he never intended to do anything about dividends, and he never intended to do anything about selfemployed people. Here are some of the questions put to the federal government by the government of Manitoba in the paper entitled "Manitoba questions on the federal government's 'Attack on Inflation' Program." I know some of the answers, so I will put them on the record in view of the minister's hesitancy to do so. The Premier of Manitoba asked:
In light of the difficulty of limiting income increases-particularly for professionals-is the federal government prepared
(1)	to make available information obtained through the income tax system to the Anti-Inflation Board?
There was no answer to that question. He continued:
(2)	to institute a special surtax through the income tax system to ensure that abuse of the guidelines by these higher income groups is kept to a minimum?
The answer to that was "No." Let me stray for a moment to read another question and to give the answer of the minister. The province of Manitoba said to the minister:
We know that a surtax put on professionals by one province is very difficult to collect. If we put a surtax on the incomes of doctors and the provinces of Alberta and Ontario do not, doctors may move from Saskatchewan to one of those provinces. We are prepared to think about that, but if we want to impose a surtax on doctors operating in the province of Saskatchewan, will you collect that surtax? We do not collect the income tax, as we have made an agreement under which you collect income taxes payable in Saskatchewan.
What was the answer of the Minister of Finance? It was "No," Mr. Speaker. We have said from the beginning that this minister has not the slightest intention of implementing an income tax policy which is fair and equitable; that this minister is bent to all the special interest groups and is prepared to let self-employed, professional people collect all they can. Let me read some of the other questions referring to professional fees. Here is one:
Are the increases in income allowed to professionals under the guidelines based on net professional income only or are professionals permitted to reduce their income for purposes of the guidelines by taking advantage of tax loopholes such as excessive capital cost allowances, interest costs, etc., on investments?
No answer from the minister. Here is another question:
Is the federal government prepared to recommend any action to curb income increases generated by current fee schedules? Examples include architects who often charge a percentage of the finished project, real estate agents and lawyers who often charge a percentage of the value on the consideration passing.
Let us take a hypothetical case. Suppose the architect in charge of that tremendous fiasco, the Olympic Games site, was a Canadian instead of a Frenchman from France. It has been reported that he is to receive a fee in the neighbourhood of $16 million. The minister would have no intention of charging surtax on that exorbitant fee. The next question was:

In light of the practical problems of having the Anti-Inflation Board deal with professional income increases is the federal government prepared to have this section of the guidelines administered by national revenue?
No answer-which of course means "No". The next question:
Will the federal government be prepared to respond to complaints re professionals who have allegedly violated the guidelines?
Mr. Speaker, from the questions we asked the minister in committee it is obvious the government will not be doing anything about most professions, like doctors, until some time in 1977 when they file their returns for their 1976 incomes. The next question was:
Will the guidelines apply the same maximum increases of $2,400 to professionals as applies to the normal wage earner?
Of course not, Mr. Speaker. The minister did not say so. If all the minister wants to do is put the guidelines on the fee schedule, obviously any relationship between the fee schedule and the actual income of the doctor, lawyer or architect is purely coincidental. For professionals the program is a farce.
Now let us look at pricing in the private sector. The province of Manitoba asked some cogent questions but received no answers from the government or from the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board. The Manitoba government spoke about the cost flowthrough rule in calculating price increases and asked:
Does this mean that the Anti-Inflation Board and the administrator can order a rollback in prices only if they can prove that the guidelines have been breached and that the breach was intentional-not due to the favourable cost developments or unusual productivity increases referred to above?
Another question on timing:
On timing, will the board be in a position to examine proposed price increases before they occur? To forestall increases which do not appear to be justifiable? Alternatively, will the only "effective enforcement" result from the examination of the firm's records two or three or four years after the fact as is the case under income taxation?
Of course, Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what is going to happen because the government has not required approval of price increases before they are imposed. Some members have been sending to the Anti-Inflation Board the examples of price increases they have received in the hundreds, and to date have not received a single reply. At the rate they are going, I suggest that will take three or four years. The government of Manitoba asked:
Is there any provision in the guidelines to prevent firms currently reaping excess profits from passing on the full brunt of any cost increases in higher prices?
Mr. Speaker, it is a very good question. The banks have just had these tremendous profits, and next year, if their costs go up, they can increase their service costs again. Let me go back to the report of the Globe and Mail in today's issue. They indicate some of the reasons the banks' profits are so high. Let me read a couple of paragraphs from the article as follows:
Other factors that helped bank profits during the year were increases in bank service charges, most of them made in the spring, and the slowing of the rapid growth in salaries and benefits costs over the year.
December 2, 1975

Later, it continues:
Another factor that helped bank profits in the latter part of the year was the ending of the 10 per cent surcharge on profits, which had lasted from May 1, 1974, to April 30, 1975.
There is no reason why the banks will not be able to again increase their service charges. Again, the minister has given no indication that he will do anything about it. As I have only a few more minutes, I will just place one more quotation on the record:
Revenue Canada has estimated that Canada is losing about $1.6 billion per year under what is called transfer pricing. Under transfer pricing, multinational firms operating in Canada purchase commodities from foreign sister corporations at a price in excess of the "market place price". The reverse also occurs-the Canadian corporation sells to its foreign sister at a price less than the "marketplace price". In both cases, the result is that the profits are diverted from Canada to a sister corporation operating elsewhere. As mentioned earlier this practice costs the Canadian treasury about $1.6 billion per year. How will the Anti-Inflation Board with its staff of 200 deal with this problem which National Revenue and its staff of thousands have not been able to resolve?
In case members opposite think that that last quotation and the statement contained in it is an exaggeration by an irresponsible socialist NDP government, let me put on the record some comments by Mr. James Gourley, the director-general of audit for Revenue Canada, in a recent speech reported in the October 31, 1975, Globe and Mail:
Canada is losing hundreds of millions of dollars a year to people and companies that avoid taxes, and a lot of it is being lost to multinational corporations using their international status to shuffle their profits out of the taxman's reach ... some of the multinationals use their intricate corporate structures to minimize the taxes they pay ...
He said he had no idea how much revenue Canada is losing through tax avoidance by multinational corporations. He guessed that missing revenue from all sources-including multinationals-might be 10 per cent of total revenue.
Estimated revenue for the current fiscal year is $27.75 billion.
Mr. Gourley has estimated the loss at more than twice the figure given by the government of Manitoba. The former minister of national revenue, now Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), said at the same meeting:
It is difficult for Canadian tax officials to decide whether the costs being charged by subsidiary companies in Canada are fair or are being inflated to boost costs and lower taxes.
A subsidiary in Canada may be supplied with products or services by its parent in another country. The subsidiary would write off those costs against its profits.
One need only look at the large multinational farm implement companies which are busier and making more money than ever before. If they are forced to observe the so-called guidelines, they will find, as Mr. Gourley and the minister said in their speeches, that it is very easy to adjust the financial transactions between the Canadian and American corporations so that the profits in Canada will not breach the guidelines.
What we are dealing with today, and will be voting on in the next few days, is a bill which interfere very drastically with the right of ordinary citizens to continue to bargain freely and collectively with their employers on their own behalf.
Anti-Inflation Act

speechtext: What is being proposed by this government are wage controls but not price controls. There will be no controls or restrictions on incomes earned through dividends, profits or any other form of income except wages and salaries. Therefore, we cannot, and will not, support such a proposal.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the debate on second reading of Bill C-73, I already called attention to the discredit drawn by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when, on October 13 last, he announced price and income controls, the very idea of which he condemned during the 1974 election. And this he did without a word of excuse for his remarks at that time. The Prime Minister spoke as the man capable of curing Canada of that terrible illness-inflation-that ruins the economy and reduces millions of Canadians to utmost abject poverty.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know of any public figure in all Canada's history discrediting himself to such a degree, without a blink, without even accepting his government's responsibility in the increasing rate of the inflationary spiral. The Prime Minister preached austerity, but taking good care to force upon others what he will not do when his own administration is involved, that is cutting right now non-essential government spending. In so doing, he could expect nothing but hostile reactions from the people he himself had warned against controls. Better still then the Leader of Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), better than anyone else in the country, the head of the government knew that a control policy was required, because he had better means and more precise instruments for economic surveying. History will never forgive him for deceiving Canadians.

The fundamental issue that this House must address itself to on third reading is an issue that runs to the very heart of our democratic system. The principle of this bill and its purpose are in line with broad public opinion at this time. Indeed, while the government is by no means providing leadership, they can at least be said to be following the leadership provided by public opinion. Just for the purpose of setting the record straight, we should note that when it came to providing leadership on the issue of price and income restraint, it was the members of this party who were prepared to level with the country a year ago.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION

speechtext:
What the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is asking for now is a blank cheque. The duration allotted for

December 2, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
the powers in the bill is, by far, an example of over playing government, and the refusal of the government to make long-term commitments relative to the control of its own spending is an example of weakening the government's hand. What the government has said and what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has said, through refusal to allow a meaningful parliamentary review of the program within a reasonable period of time, is that they do not believe the program will stand the test of time; they do not believe it will gain sufficient support in an 18-month period. It is not surprising that such lack of confidence is contributing to hesitancy on the part of certain provinces when it comes to participating as fully as the government would like. It is, therefore, with regret and with sorrow that we shall have to vote against this bill. We do so because, clearly, it is the only option left open to this party if we are to keep faith with the principle we advanced to the nation on this issue.
There is a significant demand in the country today for sound economic leadership. It has to be leadership that is based on trust, moulded through consistency and founded upon compassion. It must be leadership which is exercised in close relation to the anxieties and economic aspirations of the people. It can be firm, but when necessary it can be flexible, too. In that respect the bill now before us, the government which drafted it, and the program which has been presented to us are a sad failure.

I have no intention, Mr. Speaker, to revive the 1974 election campaign, and God knows I have excellent recollections of it. But I cannot help pointing out that if the Prime Minister had had any decency, he would either have asked for a new mandate from the Canadian people he deliberately deceived a year ago, or he would have urged the Governor General to designate another head of government. As far as fighting inflation is concerned, the Prime Minister has fallen into total discredit, and he knows it. I will not endorse here extravagant reactions by labour leaders, nor justify them for speaking of general protest strikes.
I hope before it is too late those labour leaders will come to their senses and ask their membership to abide by the law. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that does not prevent me from sympathizing with the humble workers ruined by inflation who for purely electoral reasons were made to believe and even promised that there would be no control. If Canadian voters cannot trust the word of the Prime Minister of the country, and they can no longer do that since October 13, to whom will they turn? I wonder, Mr. Speaker.
Only one party leader in this Parliament can talk of price and income control with increased and undeniable moral authority, and that is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who was not afraid to tell the truth to Canadians. History will do him justice for not sacrificing his convictions to power and not taking advantage of the credulity of the people of this country for purely electoral reasons. The respect the Leader of the Opposition now commands shows that Canadians recognize in him the true leader of this country. The other leader-the one who exercises power or looks as if he exercises it-is nothing

but a poor puppet lost in his own contradictions. A discredited Prime Minister, a discredited government, a discredited program, that is what the country is down to at the time when Bill C-73 is about to be passed by the Parliament of Canada. But, as the Leader of the Opposition stated, the Conservative Progressive party does not want to become an accomplice to a sham legislation aimed at imposing genuine economic dictatorship over all sectors of activity for three years and putting in the hands of bureacrats without any popular mandate the administration of a legislation whose faults are so obvious.

The government is as rigid and unbending as ever. It is a government which has performed a total about-turn on the issue of controls. They scoffed at our temporary freeze proposal, yet now they bring in a three-year program which makes our temporary freeze look restrictive indeed. I do not know that it is fair to say the government is totally inconsistent. While it may be inconsistent in its economic policy, it remains consistent in its authoritarianism, rigidity and insensitivity. It is these very qualities which have weakened the economy of our nation, attacked the private sector and contributed to the alienation of organized and unorganized labour.
Only this government could take a program calling for short-term controls and turn it into a long-term emasculation of the free market and the collective bargaining process. Only this government could combine insensitivity to a problem, on one hand, with alienation and extremism on the other. Only this government could turn the private sector, labour and other jurisdictions against it so quickly and so conclusively. While some seek to build a national anti-inflation front, the government appears to be fragmenting what front there is, day by day.
I once observed, in a speech in this House, that the former minister of finance had done for economic stability what Jack the Ripper did for door-to-door canvassing. I say today that this new program may do for controls what Eddie Shack did for the gentlemanly game of hockey. There is no need to radicalize our nation's economy into warring and distrustful segments. There is no need to create new fears and new suspicions for the working man and woman. What must be done is very simple: an example of restraint, self-denial, compassion and decisiveness must serve as the values around which an embattered economy can rally. To date, this government has not given Canadians anything around which they can rally, or anything in which they can believe.
Part of tackling inflation is changing people's beliefs about how bad inflation is and how bad it will become in the future. The three-year limit on this program is a very sad commentary of the incapacity of this government to hold out real, immediate hope for the people of this country. What the three-year limit means is that a substantial element of this program might only be changed through a change in the government of Canada. That, Mr. Speaker, is a corner that this government should not paint itself into. If it insists on wielding the brush, then those who are opposed to economic injustice might well be prepared to open a can or two in 1978 to help finish the job. Today in this House, at this stage of the bill, the choice is the
December 2, 1975

government's, and they are laughing about it. In three years' time, the choice will be the people's.
Mr. Speaker, the first mistake of this government was to refuse, probably because of its self-sufficiency, to impose the price and wage freeze for a 60-to-80-day period. It is something that every economist recommended. The chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, a man highly respected in Liberal circles, this chairman, the Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin himself, said a few days ago before the Standing Committee on Finances, Trade and Economic Affairs that a temporary price freeze would have allowed him to see better where he was going and to organize the board with no concern other than making it as efficient as possible and without having to decide readily on more than 140 cases submitted to him without knowing formally under which regulations the board will have to function. Mr. Pepin, could not grant this government a better certificate of incompetence.
Canadians are paying a high price for the self-sufficiency of their Prime Minister a Prime Minister who neither accepts the advice of anyone nor admits that he could be wrong.
Since this bill was passed on second reading, the opposition tried without success to convince the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to limit the implementation of Bill C-73 to 18 months. This request was not aimed at harrassing this government because the Progressive Conservative Party was the first to recommend controls as a measure against inflation. It was made, as so well put by the hon. member for Joliette, in a spirit of wisdom and equity for the Canadian consumers, so that after that period their representatives might undertake a total review of conditions to determine to what extent inflation control was a failure.
In spite of what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said, the opposition did not ask that inflation be checked within 18 months. With this government, we all know that it would be impossible. We are ready, and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) confirmed it to extend the government mandate for another 18-month period, if necessary, but we do not wish to give the government full power, when it even denies us the smallest indication on the nature of the regulations governing the Anti-Inflation Board. Why should we be less demanding than the provinces themselves which have deferred their approval of the government plan because they do not want to make blind commitments?
If the government had the least democratic sense-but God knows it lost it a long time ago-it would have accepted the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition and would have associated all parliamentarians to a legislation which, in spite of its deficiencies, would have had the merit on being unanimously approved. Not only does the government refuse to confide in Parliament with regard to the regulations, not only does it refuse to submit its economic policy to a review after 18 months, but it creates extremely disturbing dislocations in a sector that is vital to social peace and economic security, because one thing has become obvious: free collective bargaining, working condi-
Anti-Inflation Act
tions are terribly restricted by Bill C-73. Not only are salary increases rigorously controlled, arbitration decisions subject to the approval of the Anti-Inflation Board, but even the other working conditions of collective agreements are not exempt from its control: the work week, social benefits, overtime pay; all those fall within the scope of the act. What else is there to negotiate?
A while ago, Mr. Speaker, I spoke of the provinces' refusal to accept the cabinet policy without knowing what the regulations will be for Bill C-73. Last week's federal-provincial conference proved the incompetence and lack of preparation of the government in its fight against inflation. Bill C-73 has hit the Canadian people like a ton of bricks: the provinces were not consulted sufficiently, neither the leaders of industry nor those of labour unions had the opportunity of expressing their views on what policy could be accepted by all sectors of the economy.
The Prime Minister, in his wisdom, in his almightiness, deemed it sufficient to say "I want" for everyone to obey implicity. The leader of the government merely forgot that we live in a democracy, that the democracy freedoms were too dearly paid by Canadians for them to sacrifice them lightly on the order of a man who as recently as a year ago managed to mislead them about the dangers our economy was exposed to.

In short, Mr. Speaker, here we are again with a bill to which the government refused to make real amendments. The government throws us as a lure this review of the legislation after 18 months. But a review of what, I ask you, a review what if not a legislation that is confused, a legislation that is obscure, troublesome, autocratic, fashioned after the very size of this government whose incompetence has become both the laughing stock and the desolation of our country?
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish that because I care too much for the well being of my fellow citizens but it is easy to predict that the government program will be a vast and dramatic failure because in too many quarters Canadians still do not accept it and because, for electoral considerations, the government destroyed its credibility in advance. You need more than just propaganda to bring people to believe in something and especially a price and income control policy. You need more than propaganda. You need competence, and the government did not show it had any. You need a minimum of moral authority, and the government does not have any at all.
On October 14 had it not been for the well-known inertia of Liberal members this government would have blown up under the indignation of all those it had misled. Mr. Speaker, to assuage his conscience the Prime Minister is now touring the country saying he is quite prepared to give up power at the next election to save the country from inflation. What generosity on his part!
What belated generosity from a man who has plunged the country into a chaotic situation, who does not even offer an apology for it and who has discredited in advance the very means by which attempts to make us believe he will rescue the Canadian economy, Mr. Speaker, let the Prime Minister spare us his rhetoric.
His defeat will come much faster than he expects. One day, even the Liberals, and I see several opposite, will be tired of such a Prime Minister and 1 can see they have difficulty restraining their applause at this thought. This government is facing the death sentence on deferment and is totally discredited. Only fear prevents it from appearing in front of the people and submitting itself to their judgment, a fear so deeply engrained that it brings a most significant grin on the faces of the few Liberal members who are present in the House.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words about Bill C-73. It has been discussed at great length. As we look over this bill, we see it has some very serious defects. No one disagreees with the suggestion that we have to control inflation. We recognize that inflation is bearing more heavily on those with low incomes, such as the pensioners and others. They are the ones who are paying the price of inflation.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said, we all know that inflation will end in disaster if it continues at the present rate. I am sure all members are also aware of the fact that in 1974 the Conservative party put forward the necessary requisites for a bill that would give full consideration to the wishes of the people who make up

Canada, including industry, labour, professional people, farmers and others right across the board. As a result, the representatives of those people would have reached a consensus with regard to the problem. At that time the Prime Minister said such a plan was unnecessary because he had inflation under control or was bringing it under control. I believe his exact words were that he was "wrestling it to the ground". The leader of the Conservative party travelled across the country informing people about the proposals of this party to control inflation. I am sure that plan would have brought about a consensus without forcing this type of legislation on the public, and could have been accomplished by agreement across Canada. This would have been something acceptable in that it had a time limit.
We now find the Prime Minister saying we must have controls. In September he said it was economic nonsense, but suddenly, one night in October, he said they were required. The sad point about all this is that the situation has deteriorated during this time to the point where no one in government now knows what they should do. Businessmen do not know how to plan, just as people in agriculture cannot plan ahead. Commerce and trade have been involved in serious strangleholds because they do not know what costs will be.
At a meeting of a committee the other day which was considering supplementary estimates, I was shocked to find out that the estimates have gone up over $1 billion in just a few months, and rising costs will be written in as a result of the inflation factor. In other words, fixed costs have gone up tremendously, in the order of 53 per cent. When that is considered in light of the inflation factor, it is alarming. As the Prime Minister has suggested, we will be going down the drain if we do not look out. How long did it take him to come to that conclusion?
We must find the answers to many questions. When is serious consideration to be given to this matter? What kind of an economy do we want? What kind of a bill must we have in order to avoid the obvious dangers? How is the bill going to work over a period of 12 months?
I could support such a measure, as members of this party have plainly stated, if we were to review the measure within a few months do determine how it is working out. But there is no way I can support a bill which contains the powers that will allow the establishment of a dictatorship and an indefinite loss of freedom. That is what could happen. We have seen it happen in other countries.
Let me make my position clear. In no way can I support a measure that could end up with the creation of a dictatorship. I will not support this bill. I do not take that position because I object to any measure of this kind, but such a measure should incorporate a review of the bill within a limited time as advocated by the Conservative party, and assist, in the end, freedom of the people.
December 2, 1975
