speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know many adjectives have been used to describe Bill C-73 and the government's anti-inflation program. This afternoon I propose to use two adjectives and to concentrate on those in respect of this particular bill and the government's program. The first adjective I could think of, which I am sure will occur to many Canadians, is "confusing". It is confusing. This is the most confusing program ever announced in this House of Commons since I came here in 1972.
I say it is confusing, first because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced there would be 1,500 corporations with 500 or more employees which would be covered in terms of wages. Now we have heard that 2,500 corporations will be covered, and there is a promise of more. It started out in the construction industry with companies which employ 20 people or more. These companies were to be covered. Perhaps the government forgot that there are over 100,000 construction companies in this country which have 20 or more employees. The board estimates there are about 5,000 of these companies which will be covered by the controls. I say that with the industry-wide wage bargaining, which the government says will be included in the guidelines and regulations, there will be up to 50,000 construction companies involved. Another point of confusion is that mortgage interest rates are not to be covered. Will real estate and stockbrokers be exempt? Some will be covered, but not all. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-
Anti-Inflation Act
donald) says it depends on their size and whether they are engaged in the construction industry.
Repeatedly the government has said that its anti-inflation program is not intended to interfere with free collective bargaining. As a matter of fact, on November 7, 1975, there was a statement by the Anti-Inflation Board that it did not intend to interfere with collective bargaining. But lo and behold, last Friday, Jean-Luc Pepin, the Chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, made a statement about the metro school board's latest offer to its teachers. This certainly destroyed meaningful collective bargaining for those parties. We have had the case of Steinberg's hiding behind the anti-inflation guideline of 10 per cent. That has ended the collective bargaining between itself and its employees. As a matter of fact, I strongly suspect the voluntary price freeze by the supermarkets which, incidentally, was started by Steinberg's, was a deliberate move to encourage customers into Steinberg's stores after they had embarked on this kind of confrontation with their employees, all the time hiding behind the government's anti-inflation program.
We have also had the case of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway and Transport Workers Union. This union approached the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and appealed to him to investigate Voyageur Colonial Limited for hiding behind the anti-inflation guidelines and refusing to negotiate meaningfully with its employees. We have heard the Minister of Labour stand up in this House and say that the paper companies are hiding behind the guidelines and refusing to negotiate in a meaningful way with their workers. It is not surprising that the trade union movement has the impression that this government is out to interfere with free collective bargaining in this country.
In respect of prices, the confusion reigns even more supreme. Apparently there are no controls on interest rates, particularly mortgage interest rates. One of my colleagues has already mentioned in the House that we might look at the latest figures with regard to the banks, reported in today's Globe and Mail in the business section. The article reads in part;
The ten chartered banks showed an after-tax balance of revenue (the equivalent of after-tax operating profit for other companies) of $182.9 million in the latest quarter, up 87.5 per cent from the corresponding quarter a year earlier.
That is what creates a credibility problem for the workers of this country whose wages are effectively controlled by this so-called anti-inflation program. But even more surprising are the factors which apparently helped the banks enjoy such a healthy profit figure. The article points out the following:
Another factor that helped bank profits in the latter part of the year was the ending of the 10 per cent surcharge on profits, which had lasted from May 1, 1974, to April 30, 1975.
The government could have extended that surcharge. It has the power to do so because it now has a majority. No longer can the government say it is shackled by a minority parliament; because it has a majority, it has the power. The government, in effect, has condoned this kind of profittaking by a large powerful group in the Canadian economic picture. There are some other factors which contribute to this very healthy profit figure. The article states that, "other factors which helped bank profits were increases in

December 2, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
bank service charges and the slowing of the rapid growth in salaries and benefits costs over the year to its employees.
It is very obvious that the government cannot say wages have been responsible for taking some of the profits of the banks. This is obvious because the banks have been very capable of controlling any increase in benefits or wages of its employees. This is an example of the kind of thing which indeed creates confusion. It is difficult for the Canadian people to understand what the government is doing. Lo and behold, after it was discovered that certain supermarkets were indeed using loopholes to skin the public, the government belatedly announced that it will monitor food prices and that in order to do so it will set up five regional offices. So far it has been admitted that over
1,000	phone calls have been received complaining of price increases.
What is also confusing is that the government has announced it will be having 200 employees in that particular department to do all the things which this program entails. How naive do they think that not only parliamentarians, but the people of Canada are to believe that a bureaucracy of 200 will do all the things it is said the program will cover.
The other confusion which prevails in respect of this program is a very important one because it deals with the cost of operating the anti-inflation program. Just the other day we had the supplementary estimates before the committee. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) was being questioned about the supplementary estimates for the Anti-Inflation Board: it is estimated that the government will require $4,863,000 up to March 31, 1976. The supplementary estimates also indicated that the number of persons employed would be 191.

We certainly have a clear indication that all the amounts of money which will be required to run this program have not yet surfaced or are being hidden very well in other departments. Obviously, it will cost a lot more than $1 million a month to operate the Anti-Inflation Board. It seems to me that the government has failed to provide accurate information as to what the actual cost of running its anti-inflation policy will be. The only accurate information made public has been through the supplementary estimates regarding the costs of the Anti-Inflation Board, and I have already referred to that figure as being $4,800,000.
As the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs pointed out, this figure does not cover the salary of support staffs of either the administrator of the program or the appeal tribunal. The administrator, under Bill C-73, along with one or more persons appointed as deputy administrators, will be covered under the Public Service Staff Relations Act and under the Public Service Employment Act. Provision is also made in this act for the appointment of staffs for the administrator and deputy administrators under the Public Service Employment Act. All of this will obviously cost a significant amount of money which has not yet been made public. The chairman of the appeal tribunal shall be paid such salary as is fixed by the governor in council, and each other member shall be paid such fees or other remuneration for his services as shall be fixed by the governor in council, according to clause 28(1) of this bill. The government has produced no figures as to what the whole cost will be. The staff for the tribunal will be handled in the same way as that of the administrator, making it another hidden cost which has not yet been disclosed to the Canadian people.
I said that I could describe this bill with two adjectives. The first is "confusing" and the second is "inappropriate". This party has said that the bill is inappropriate at the moment in Canada. On close analysis of the current economic situation one finds little evidence that inflation is
December 2, 1975

getting worse. As a matter of fact, there are signs that the economy is improving. This is borne out by a global economic survey done by Newsweek in conjunction with the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Econometrics Forecasting Association in September. I want to quote from their survey as reported in the Citizen issue of November 24, 1975, which reads as follows:
It predicts that the United States would lead the recovery and continue in an upward movement through 1976 and into 1977... includes an over-all look at the world economy as well as individual forecasts for 14 of the world's most industrialized, non-communist countries as of the third quarter of 1975.
It says world trade, which declined probably more than 6 per cent so far this year, "should pick up more than 5 per cent in 1976 and by almost 10 per cent in 1977".
It says world production, measured by the growth of the gross domestic product-the gross national product less payments of wages, interest, rent, profits and other income items paid abroad-"should be on a 4 per cent growth path or better in 1976-and this rate ought to accelerate to 6 per cent in 1977".
Inflation, the survey says should drop to "a mere 6 per cent or less in 1977".
So why did the government bring in this grotesque piece of legislation? Because the government, at the urgings of their boardroom friends, want to protect their high profittaking, and to do this wage costs must be cut down. The percentage of the national income accounted for by wages and salaries fell from 72.8 per cent in 1970 to 67 per cent in the first half of 1974. Since the middle of last year, however, the picture has changed. Labour's share increased to 69.4 per cent by the end of 1974, and by the middle of this year rose to 70.8 per cent. Big business, on the other hand, had its profits and interest fall to 21.1 per cent by the end of 1974, and to 20.1 per cent by the middle of this year.
This shift, which has by no means yet carried labour up to the share it had achieved in 1970 and which, incidentally, is quite comparable to the U.S. experience, has taken place because of an increase in the militancy of workers expressed in high wage demands and increased strikes. It has taken place in a context, however, where due to the worldwide capitalist recession, and especially the recession in the United States, Canadian corporations have convinced the government, despite a higher rate of inflation in other countries, that they cannot raise their prices to protect their profit margins if they are to remain competitive in the international markets. They have obviously convinced the government of a squeeze in profits, which is not yet particularly marked but which the government is apparently determined to prevent occurring, hence its wage restraint policy.
If we have any illusions about Jean-Luc Pepin's desire to control profits, listen to Mr. Arthur Donner, an economist with Research Securities, speaking at a meeting of Institutional Investors on October 23, 1975.
Donner told a meeting that the controls on profits and dividends seem to be much stricter than they originally appeared.
However, he doubts they will be applied very strictly since he would be surprised to see Jean-Luc Pepin come down hard on business.
He certainly would be very surprised, and I think we all would be very surprised, if Mr. Pepin came down very hard on corporate profits. We all know where he stands in that regard.
Anti-Inflation Act
In that speech he also noted that the major influence on Canada's lower inflation rate next year will be the lower rate of inflation in the United States, not controls. It seems only logical that when the inflation rate in the United States goes up, it affects our economy; and in a similar fashion, if the rate there goes down, it will obviously go down here. If we have any doubt about the loyalties of Beryl Plumptre and where her heart lies, we ought to have no difficulty in that matter because this is what she told a group of Canadians recently:
The board will have to show restraint with the companies and their profits. After all, we need profits to provide jobs and investment for more growth and more jobs.
Obviously, the biases of the two most important people on the Anti-Inflation Board have become known before they have even started operating the program. High rates of inflation are being experienced in only very specific areas such as food, energy and shelter. In most other areas inflation is moderate. Yet we find many of these specific areas are totally, or in large measure, exempt from the controls announced by the government.
Let us consider energy for a moment. It is interesting to note a speech made by Mr. Clifford Jutlah. He is an economist who works for the Ontario ministry of treasury, economics and intergovernmental affairs. Speaking to the founding meeting of the Canadian Petroleum Association of Canada, he said:
Higher oil and gas prices cost Ontario 22,000 jobs last year, 16,000 jobs this year, and an expected 19,000 jobs next year ... higher oil and gas prices can be blamed for one-third of the inflation of the past two years, and triggered the current recession in Canada ... the increases over the past couple of years, which have seen wellhead prices for oil triple and those for natural gas more than quadruple, have increased the country's fuel bill by $3 billion a year ... rising fuel prices pushed the consumer price index up 3.5 per cent in 1974, about one-third of the year's inflation.
Yet we find that particular aspect of the Canadian way of life-energy-exempt from the provisions of the guidelines. So there we have an expert economist in the Ontario government pinpointing an area where inflation has been most rampant. But we are going to leave that alone in the guidelines; we are not going to touch it. The Minister of Finance admitted in this House that controls on food prices would be difficult. The question of being able to control the pricing activities of multinational corporations has also been concededly him. There are no possible means available to monitor those prices. The minister admitted that fact in committee when we discussed the matter of transfer pricing. As for housing, the government did not move in on land speculators, nor did it touch mortgage interest rates. I have already referred to the profits the banks have recently declared. Just imagine, we hung Dick Turpin for that kind of thing! Even though housing costs have contributed much to the level of inflation in Canada, we continue to exempt interest rates, specifically mortgage interest rates, from any kind of controls.
As a matter of fact, talking to some of the teachers who were up on the Hill today, one comment came back again and again, and that is that if the government is prepared to control escalating costs such as housing and fuel, they would be very prepared to accept controls on their wages; they would not take any increases at all if the government could assure them that there would be effective controls and no skyrocketing increases in those particular items.

However, the government has chosen not to interfere with that sector at all.
Where else is inflation in Canada being fuelled? No less a person than Mrs. Sylvia Ostry, deputy minister of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, pinpointed it. She was speaking to the Empire Club in Toronto on October 30, 1975. She is one of the government's own, and the government does not even listen to what she says. By the way, she was the chief statistician in Statistics Canada. This is what she said to the Empire Club in Toronto: Business concentrations in Canada have undermined efficiency and fuelled inflation.
She went on to say:
As well, there is considerable evidence that prices in concentrated industries are less responsive to changes in the general level of business activity.
She also said that there is a "disturbing level of concentration in the Canadian economy." She pointed out the following:
A 1965 government study showed that the 50 largest companies in Canada accounted for 36 per cent of total manufacturing value-added. By comparison, the 50 largest companies in the United States accounted for 25 per cent.
She also said:
Despite the highly concentrated structure of Canadian industry, production units in this country tend to be excessively diversified, are often undersized, and typically unable to exploit potential economies that are available from longer production runs.
All these remarks I have read into the record have not referred to wages fuelling inflation; they have referred to such items as housing, fuel costs and monopolies-and these are the particular areas the government has not touched at all. The government has said it will deal with monopolies in part two of the anti-combines legislation, which is off somewhere in the future, probably at the end of this so-called three year run of the program; but it is not going to touch that baby because when it starts doing that it touches its friends in the corporate boardrooms. It is easier to control little people who may or may not be organized in unions. However, we will talk about that later.
The Minister of Finance and government economists, as well as others knowledgeable in these matters, have said that higher productivity is the key to beating inflation. Now we have to work our way out of inflation. When we look at plant capacity in Canada, we see that it has been declining over the past year to the point where it is now less than 85 per cent. I think it is around 80 per cent. Obviously, people are not trying to take more from the economy than it is capable of producing. The argument is that people are greedy, but that is a common denominator: it is a common human element, and this program will not alter that. That argument is to divert attention from the real problems.
Obviously, this economy is not operating at full capacity. There are 700,000 people in this country who are unemployed. Did 700,000 people make themselves unemployed? It was the direct action of this government between 1968 and 1972 which created the present level of unemployment. The unemployed did not ask to be put on unemployment insurance benefits. The government did this, and it will do so again with this program. It is not an accident that the

government is now redefining the unemployment rate which is acceptable in Canada under the unemployment insurance bill which is before a committee at the moment.

100.000	of those 700,000 people back to work, the impact that would have on the economy. Mr. Speaker, it is well known to the House that I did not vote for this legislation on second reading. I think the House has a right to know why I took that position. This is the first opportunity that I have been given to express these views. First, I wish to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who spoke yesterday put his finger on what will eventually become the key issue in this whole discussion. The question of taking away the freedom of people must always be the number one issue before any parliamentary government.

Anti-Inflation Act
I would not suggest for a moment that there are not times when you have to take away the freedom of the people for necessary public purposes. I recall the last war, when the nation, generally speaking, enthusiastically supported the loss of our freedom so that we could better fight that war. I vividly recall that near the end of the war, when the tide was turning in our favour, it was very difficult to keep the morale of the people high and to maintain the self-imposed disciplines that they had to impose on themselves to carry out this loss of freedom. I saw a great nation like the British become demoralized at the end of the war. The black market spread all through the economy and the respect for law declined in that once great nation.
I am not going to develop the theme of freedom after what the right hon. member for Prince Albert said yesterday, but I am sure that over the years to come this will be quoted as one of the examples of where a government, without legitimate cause, moved in the direction of restricting the freedom of our people in the economic field.
I suggest you can learn a lot by watching the method of operation of a leader or a government. My mind goes back to the election of 1968. With deliberate planning, the election was called on a Tuesday, instead of the usual Monday, so that the election could be held the day after the St. Jean Baptiste celebrations in the city of Montreal. In those celebrations, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) deliberately provoked the animosity of the people and had bottles and cans thrown at him. This had the effect, on the eve of the election, of polarizing the people on an issue that was really not involved in the election. I recall with deep sadness watching that demonstration over television which I could not help believing was not accidental.
I saw that technique used in 1968. I saw it repeated in 1970. I was not a member of this chamber at that time. I joined a group of people over at St. John's cathedral to protest the War Measures Act on the grounds that there was not sufficient challenge to the safety of the state to bring on the military to control a few social drop-outs in the city of Montreal. When the evidence is brought out, it will indicate conclusively that, because of a few frightened politicians, we put the whole majesty of the forces of this nation to corralling a few lawbreakers that you would ordinarily send a junior sergeant over to settle. That method of operation used in 1970 rallied the whole nation behind the Prime Minister because the people are taught to believe that you must always respect the leader of your country. They are taught that when he says the country is in danger, you rally behind him.
There was a third occasion. When the election was called in 1974, it was the government, aided and abetted by the New Democratic Party, that went on the attack and labelled the leader of the Conservative party as the devil to be aware of because he was going to bring in wage and price controls. In nearly six weeks of that compaign, in both official languages of this country we heard the phrase "there is going to be a freeze on your wages." So successful was that indoctrination of the minds of people listening to the media that the labour vote of our big cities, particularly Vancouver and Toronto, voted Liberal to save themselves from this desperate freeze for 90 days. The leader of

the NDP who supported that type of strategy paid a heavy price for his mistake, as did our leader.
Our leader, who had taken the stand which he did, announced that stand in this House many months before the election. After the election he stood up before his party and accepted all the blame. He is retiring from public life, not honoured by success in the field of electoral victory but honoured by this nation because he tried to paint the picture of truth in the hope of getting a national decision. At this moment in Canada's history, if a general election were being held today and this man was the leader of our party, he would be the prime minister after the election.

However, such is not the case. What we are faced with here is another of the techniques of confrontation. There is no question in the minds of most of us who know what goes on here that there has been a strong movement, for many years, in a select group within our civil service which holds to the view that individuals in Canada are not competent to make decisions for themselves. They do not believe that the farmers should be allowed free decision-making. We saw that in a raft of legislation in the session of 1970. They do not believe that business knows how to make decisions. There is continual interference in that sector.
However, with this particular move at this time, knowing the pressure of the civil service for its planned system of society, the government acquiesced to them. The Prime Minister immediately reverted to his traditional method of operation, namely, confrontation. In this announcement the Prime Minister deliberately went out to confront the big labour unions of this country and to pose as the defender of the great majority against the great barons of labour. Listening to the speeches of the NDP, I can sympathize entirely with the philosophy of what they are trying to say. It is wrong in a nation like Canada to try to make any segment of the economy or any minority group the target of a government's animosity. I do not necessarily agree with all I have heard from the New Democratic Party in this debate, but on this question of the fairness of it, and what is being done to the democratic system, whether you are attacking the St Jean Baptiste Society, whether you are appealing to the fears of the nation about law and order in Montreal in 1970, whether you are frightening the labour votes in 1974 and then turning around and attacking the labour leaders in 1974, the method of operation is consistent, and that is not good for democracy. That is the number one key issue. You do not take away freedom lightly; you do not apply a system of controls lightly. It is only when a nation is in desperate straits.
I spoke in the House on this subject two years ago. We were allowed by the Chair to have an all night debate and I put forward a series of proposals I thought the government could adopt to attack inflation. There were five proposals. I am not going to quote the whole thing tonight. I would just like to quote a concluding paragraph which can be found on page 6538 of Hansard of September 13, 1973. These are my own words:
December 2, 1975

It is not an accident that the Conservative party, surely the last party that would ever go for controls, should come out and say we see no recourse but for a 90-day freeze, then one and a half or two years for controls to ensure stability so we can move forward with our long and short range policies. Whenever the Conservative party accepts that position, great is the danger to the nation because in the long run controls are inflationary. You have to get out of them as fast as you can However, you cannot put in these policies and make these changes unless there is that economic stability. That is what I am asking the House to consider.
That was the anguished conclusion I reached over two years ago at a time when we were in a demand-pull type of inflation added on top of the cost-push. We had to put in that freeze to give us time to bring in a budget attacking the fundamental causes of inflation on several fronts simultaneously.
The reason for selective controls is obvious. You might find corporations, big business, big unions not willing to follow too quickly some of the directions laid down in the budget, which had to offer tax incentives and positive inducements, not restrictive controls. We needed those selective controls with the authority of the provinces, since only the provinces have constitutional authority to interfere with property and civil rights. That view I put on the record in the House, Mr. Speaker, over two years ago.
The bill before us now makes no effort to get after the fundamental causes of inflation. In addition to being a direct attack on a group, the working people, it is also a direct attack on the constitution of this nation. I have read the speeches given in this debate from the very beginning up to last night, and I attended here today. Three or four speakers have mentioned the constitutional aspects, but I say with deep feeling that this country has not been done right by. No member on either side has made any real effort to put before the people of Canada the seriousness of the constitutional attack on the provinces this bill represents.

I am simply referring to the speeches I have read. I think members much better qualified than I should be the ones to lay before the people the dangers which are inherent in this bill in terms of our constitutional rights and privileges.
Forgetting party for the moment, when you restrict or control the citizen there must be a good reason, and the question I ask is this: does Bill C-73 attack inflation and is the inflation so great that the nation is in mortal peril? That is the question I put before all of us as Canadians. My first answer to that question, from my own point of view, is that the bill does not fight inflation. This bill in every one of its terms legislates inflation. For example, it legislates that the working man can get no more than 8, 10 or 12 per cent increase per year on his income. Let us call it 10 per cent. In fact we all know that this is the amount which will be forthcoming. We have, by the very nature of human nature, legislated that the increase in the cost to society of working people's wages will be 10 per cent.
Still on the question of legislating inflation, we have said in the legislation that as far as prices are concerned they will be based on cost. If costs go up 10 per cent or 20 per cent to compensate for the increased costs built into the system in the last two or three years, then the busi-
Anti-Inflation Act
nessman is allowed to take his profit on the basis of that cost. So we have a cost-plus situation. This was what hurt us so badly during the control system during and after the war.
The story is told that businessmen used to come down to the hotel here regularly and after a hard day of sitting around government offices trying to meet somebody, they would go down and have a good meal at night. They would eat well and drink well. And when a large bill would be presented by the waiter at the end of the meal they all fought for the bill. One man would say, "Let me have that bill, my company is in the 50 per cent bracket and it only costs us half the bill." Another fellow would say, "Give me that bill. I am on an individual tax rate. I will get 90 per cent back if I pay the bill." But the guy who always won the right to pay the bill was the guy who said, "I am on a cost-plus contract and I will make 10 per cent."
This is exactly what has been legislated in the bill as far as prices are concerned. You have legislated cost-plus, which means you have legislated inflation in prices, all in the hope that prices and wages will not go above the level of 10 per cent which is the objective.
A year or so from now hon. members will find my statements to be true-that inflation has maintained its level around 10 to 20 per cent. So the first thing I have to say about Bill C-73 is that it legislates inflation, it does not fight inflation.
My second point, which I have touched on already, is that I suspect that this bill in the normal sense has to be considered unconstitutional. It has been mentioned that there is no preamble appealing to the good order clause in the constitution. What has not been mentioned sufficiently, in my judgment, is that most wages and prices are completely within the field of the provinces. This bill says that it is not binding upon Her Majesty in the right of the provinces or upon Her Majesty in right of the municipalities, yet the government is systematically sitting down with one province after another and conniving together to get around the constitution of the country. As some provinces are now indicating, the legislation will not work because of its unconstitutional nature.
My third point is that the bill is pure public relations. Even before the announcement was made to the nation we discovered from reading the insider accounts, in the magazine that reports for the government to the people of Canada, that it wanted, first of all, a public relations man. Only later did it go for the other people to head up the program. When you see a government heading for the top public relations man it could find, over whom it had a hold, and it brings him back, and then later it figures out who will head up the program, then you can understand why I say this is a pure public relations operation.
We know the senior mandarins of the civil service wanted some planned controls on a permanent basis for many years. We also know there are individuals in the government who are opposed, and have been opposed, to controls, and who know that they will not work. Therefore what we have here is an effort to go out on a public relations war, using as the first target the big labour barons, so as to try to unite the country against this

particular group. There are lots of reasons that the government could put forward for uniting against them, and in this way they hope to get the support of the country for this unworkable program.
I think every member of the House knows that this past year the government had no intention of employing wage and price controls, but what triggered it off was the departure of the former minister of finance. With his departure panic set in, and both the caucus and cabinet joined in pressing for action that would carry out what the civil service had wanted all along. I put this point before you, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that we will know the real enemy here. There are some people in this country who want a planned, controlled system to work all of the time.
My fourth point about what I do not like in Bill C-73 is that its economics are so brutal. Many studies are available from people much more learned than I, written in very involved English, showing that when there is, say, 5 per cent inflation in prices, governments get a lot more money than the 5 per cent. One study shows that 13 per cent accumulates to government whenever prices rise by 5 per cent. Transposing that to 12 per cent inflation, about 30 per cent goes to government. If one looks at the income of the government these past three or four years, without there being any serious change in the tax level, one finds a tremendous flood of money flowing into government coffers. It is easy to see why governments have a vested interest in inflation; they like it because they get more money to bring in more programs.
Even though the government has accepted the principle of indexing and has applied it partially, some of the studies that have been published indicate that it is government that is the big winner in inflation. We should think seriously not only of the civil servant who believes sincerely in a planned economy; we should also think of the fact that governments, mortal as they are want to get all the money they can. The main reason that they do not want to fight inflation is that they are the biggest beneficiaries. That is the point I want to make.
I do not think it is right just to condemn this legislation for what it is, bad legislation, without putting forward some form of alternative that is credible and reasonable. I have done this before, but I will do it again. A real antiinflation plan can be put forward, and it is not new. I would think that the great majority of rational minded people, if they had to list the causes of modern day inflation, would put government spending or costs as number one. I have read the speeches of three or four or more speakers, and the Leader of the Opposition pointed that fact out over and over again.
When I speak of government costs I do not want to leave the impression that the only thing you can do to cut costs is to cut down on things like the Prime Minister's swimming pool. That is pure nibbling at the problem. I am talking about the fact that 70 per cent to 80 per cent of the costs of the federal government are locked-in costs; I think they call them statutory costs. No one has been making any effort to find out how we are going to cope with these open-ended policies that bring increasing tax burdens on the shoulders of the people in order to fuel these funds that grow and grow.

When I speak of a real anti-inflation plan to meet rising government costs, I am not talking about the 20 per cent to 30 per cent that you nibble off here and there. I am referring to the basic problem. I am not talking about negative deterrents in these programs; I am saying that enough knowledge has been collected over the last 30 years to turn the philosophy of these programs around and, through positive, dynamic approaches, cut the programs down compared with what they are today, and without taking away one single service that the people want.
I happen to know that one of these proposals was made in 1948, which is a long time ago, but no government has acted on it. I say it is about time we began to reassess the fundamental philosophy of the statutory programs that we have and which the people want. I am prepared at any time to put these programs forward in detail, with the quantitative evidence behind them, to show that they can and will work. In other words, government costs are the number one target.
When this party put forward an amendment in committee to the effect that the government should restrict itself to some 10 per cent in the matter of increased government spending, as it is so restricting the individuals of this country, the amendment was refused by the government. That is conclusive proof that the government has no intention of applying the same kind of controls to itself as it is applying to the working man. The refusal of this amendment convinced the Conservative opposition that there was no intention on the government's part of being sincere about reducing inflation. Since the government is the chief culprit in this rising tide of inflation, unless it takes some action inflation will continue.
I should have liked the amendment to go further and limit the government's income to 10 per cent. That would be the largest guarantee that expenses would be cut down.
The second point in a real anti-inflation plan has to be the question of getting at interest rates, and this again was mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition in his speeches. Once more, let me assure the House that there are positive ways of getting at this. These figures are not original and they are not precise, but they are accurate. If you buy a house or a new home today, and take out a $50,000 mortgage, and that is not unusual in our big cities, at 12 per cent for 30 years, before you finish paying for that home you will have paid out over $200,000. You will have paid $150,000 interest on a $50,000 home.
I have already said in this House that in the way we are presently financing the oil sands development in Alberta, with the federal government, the Ontario government, and the Alberta government participating with private industry, it is costing $11 a barrel to produce the oil. If we adopted the old fashioned method of financing, going back thousands of years, we could reduce that cost of oil to $3 a barrel. About $8 per barrel goes in interest, adding to the cost of the consumer and forcing the workingman to go out on strike for higher wages in order to meet all these costs.
If we want lower interest rates surely there is someone on the government side who can figure out a way of speeding up the payment for a house mortgage. If a person were to pay that $50,000 mortgage in ten years his interest
December 2, 1975

would not be $150,000, but would be $27,000. Surely there must be somebody on the government benches who has the muscle and the will to talk with civil servants and say he wants a housing program that cuts these costs to the people who want to buy homes. Surely there is a way of cutting these interest costs.
If we can cut these costs down to the point where a person is given an incentive to pay off the mortgage quickly, then he will get his house for $77,000 in ten years and would be saving himself $123,000. You would have a double advantage because the money would be turning over faster and faster and the velocity of capital flow would be improved, thus in turn decreasing interest rates.
If we are short of capital for all these things we want today we can get it in two ways-one is to save more money, and the other is to speed up capital flow. If you speed up capital flow three times this is the same as tripling the money supply, and if you triple your money supply you decrease interest rates. If the government does not have anyone on its side who knows how to do this I can tell you that there are plenty on this side who do. We regret that we have to sit here in the opposition another four years waiting for those unscrupulous people, who will adopt any issue to win an election, to come up with these ideas to help the people of this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The
third point in this battle against inflation is money supply, and this has been dealt with by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I will not bother once again with decimal point accuracy, but will just give the rough figures.
During the years when Mr. Pearson was Prime Minister the money supply increased from $13 billion under the previous administration to $18 billion. We had inflation rising from 11A per cent to 3 per cent. During the years of the present administration the money supply has reached $65 billion, and has been held there for the last few months. Surely with all the evidence of the co-relation between increasing money supply and rising inflation there must be some awareness on the part of the treasury benches that there must be a responsibility on those people elected by the people of Canada to give directions to the Bank of Canada.
Obviously we need a formula based on the gross national product to make sure there is no shortage of money for legitimate growth, but we also need a formula that includes a factor to cover the velocity of money flow, something which is missing from any type of formula the Bank of Canada has used in the last 30 years.
This is not the type of thing that you discuss in detail in the House of Commons, but it is the type of thing a responsible government should be directing the bank of Canada to carry out, and that is, stopping this business of flooding the country with money and raising interest rates at the same time. There has to be a positive policy in respect of money supply. It does not have as much effect as people think, but it is a requirement.
The fourth point in this positive program is the matter of land costs. I do not think the people in cities have to look
Anti-Inflation Act
any further than areas within 20 or 30 miles of those cities to see what the basic inflationary force has been. If you go back to the year 1955 you will see that the value of land around Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver was not too different from what it was 20 years before, but in the last 20 years that land value has escalated beyond all comprehension. This land value escalation has added to the cost of homes, even before inflation hit building costs.
Say that in the Toronto area the average worker's small home cost $19,000 in 1964, just at the beginning of land cost increases. In 1974 the average cost was $57,000, approximately a 300 per cent increase in a decade in the cost of purchasing a home in the Toronto area. Since then other cities have risen to challenge Toronto in this regard.
If the government wants to do anything to reduce the most oppressive costs to city people it should first take these programs which it has now under the CMHC Act, the National Housing Act, and other statutes, and hit these programs on the nose interestwise, not tomorrow but now. What has happened in the last ten or 15 years I think will continue to be the cost-push plight of our economy for many years to come. This has to be stopped and corrected, and the provinces have to be participants in this. If we are going to help city people get their basic costs down, that must be one of the main thrusts.
The fifth point in this program is a sensitive one, and one in which the NDP will be interested. At this point in time it is popular in Canada to say that the number one person who should be blamed for inflation is the labouring man. I do not accept that. With rising land costs the labouring man is forced to get more money, and has had no choice but to go to his union leaders and say, "Now, look, we do not want 30-cents an hour increase, we want $1.30 an hour to catch up". Generally speaking, the labouring man is not the primary cause of inflation. He is fifth in the line.
The labouring man in trying to catch up was doing what every other group was trying to do. What went wrong, of course, was that when the labouring man caught up on a 2-year contract he got behind again, so the smart labour leaders began to say, "Back me and I will get you ahead". So we have, in addition to the catch-up procedures by labour, the get-ahead concept, and to that degree I agree with the general public that labour leaders have to be held responsible.
These leaders were doing this because of increased government costs, higher taxes, increased land costs, rising interest rates and everything else. Labour is not the only partner to inflation. We all know that, and I object very strongly to any attempt to single out one single group as being at fault. We cannot fault any single group, big business or big labour, for trying to get ahead of the game rather than just trying to catch up. I point out also that I do not believe we will solve this problem of inflation by confrontation with any group, business or labour.
We must face the fact that our technique of collective bargaining which ends up as a confrontation technique is costing labour, management, and the consumer dearly. We all suffer.
We had a debate here in the fall of 1974 concerning strikes on the west coast. Why has there not been any noise

Anti-Inflation Act
about the west coast this year? It seemed that there had been one strike after another on the west coast, and then it was very quiet. I know the reason, and I hope the whole country knows the reason. The men who work and the men who administer business out there have become sick and tired of their both losing money because of these constant confrontations and strikes. They are trying to find a way out of it. The key way is through productivity in which labour shares the advantage with management, productivity in respect of which the consumer does not suffer. Productivity is one of the main ways to attack inflation.
If we were to chart the productivity of our country and the country to our south, the United States, we would find that our productivity has fallen off in the last two years in a steady downward curve while the Americans are fighting their way out of inflation not with controls but by an upward productivity trend in the economy. They are coming out of their situation. There is some hesitation involved in the process, but they are coming out of it. I say so far as this party is concerned we do not believe in confrontation between labour and management. We believe in the common-sense approach of finding out what the situation is in each particular case, and by using the device of productivity with security of tenure for the working man, portability of his pension so that he may move around, portability of insurance rights, and more particularly participation in the decisions, we are prepared to put forward a positive program to achieve non-confrontation in the labour field.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad even at this late stage in the debate to have an opportunity to speak against the third reading of this so-called anti-inflation bill. I do not want to repeat the reasons already advanced. My colleagues and others in this House have made very clear in their views, which I share, that the provisions of this bill are unfair and inequitable.
The government can send squads of ministers across Canada asking for consensus, but until they are able to show in detail that the control over prices is as firm and as effective as control over wages and salaries, there is no way in which they can secure support. I do not at all mean to suggest that inflation is not an extremely serious evil. Nor do I wish to imply that the government ought to have taken no action. The fact of the matter is that the action which it has taken is ineffective and unjust, and is therefore worse than useless.
I wish to concentrate on some of the questions which have not been developed very much during this debate. First, in my view this bill is a negation of parliamentary democracy. It signals the abdication of parliament. I know of course that in many modern democracies the handing over of power to the executive by the elected parliament has proceeded apace, but I venture to say that never before has this process reached such an overwhelming and absolute degree.
What does the legislation say? In effect it says that the cabinet or the governor in council has unlimited power to make, reverse, or revoke the guidelines affecting wages, salaries, incomes, profits, prices both public and private, and affecting individuals and corporate business. I say that such a power handed over to the cabinet in effect means 
that parliament will not have and does not have any effective control over the legislative process.
I have re-read the bill very carefully and it would seem that there is no attempt to limit or circumscribe in any way the content of the guidelines. Indeed machinery is set up for the Anti-Inflation Board, the administrator, and the appeal tribunal-and I shall want to speak some more about this later-including penalties of $10,000 or two years, or both on summary conviction, and not less than $10,000 or five years' imprisonment when the offence is tried as an indictable offence.
What are the offences? No one knows. Largely they are put forward in the vague form of failure to comply with the act and, presumably, the controls. What are the offences under the guidelines? Who knows? We have never been told. We are to provide penalties, but basically they are for offences which are indefinite, the content of which we have never been advised.
I appreciate that government supporters have little option but to support this legislation. I appreciate also that this amorphous piece of legislation is such that it cannot be rationally amended by parliament, although I always thought it was the duty of parliament to amend something that cannot be gotten hold of in any other way. I know the private members on the government side have no power, authority, or position other than just to go ahead and kindly support the bill. We say all the more blame falls on the government for placing these members in the position of emasculating if not destroying parliament. I say that feature alone would be enough reason to oppose this bill vigorously.
The next point I want to make has to do with the constitution. That was referred to by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), and also earlier by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). This matter has received very little discussion. I want to protest that a bill of such importance in dealing with our fundamental law and constitution, which in effect provides for widespread invasion of provincial rights, should be brought forward here and brushed aside so far as the constitutional argument is concerned.
What are we told? I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in answer to a question said that someone in the Department of Justice gave an opinion. We do not know who the person was, or his reasons. We have one of the greatest constitutional issues ever to come before parliament and the courts which is brushed aside because some anonymous official has said it is all right and that we should not ask questions about it. I think that is a shameful failure to pay any attention to the constitution which, after all, is the very basis for our existence as a country.
Let no one say it is clear or obvious that parliament has the right to step in and regulate prices, wages, salaries, profits, and all these things without any relation whatever to those things which normally have been regarded as within provincial constitutional power. I know this House does not appreciate a lecture on the subject of the constitution. It would probably be very good for some members to have such a lecture, but I do not intend to give it at this time.
December 2, 1975

I will tell the House, and perhaps it is immodest for me to do so, that I argued two cases in the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council which involved constitutional issues. I argued dozens of cases in the Supreme Court of Canada on constitutional issues, and many cases in the Ontario Court of Appeal, and during that process I learned a little bit about the constitution. Now I want to say that this particular issue is one that is not clear one way or the other. Many authorities dealing with this matter could argue that legislation of this sort comes under trade and commerce, section 91(2) of the British North America Act. I do believe this legislation goes far beyond any normal regulation of trade and commerce.
It is suggested that it may be justified as an emergency. I am far from saying that inflation might not reach a state of emergency which would justify emergency action, but what do we have? We have the government itself, in the preamble-which is always looked at by the courts to determine the real basis and substance of the legislation- making no reference to an emergency, either in precise terms or in its content. It is merely stated in a mild way that inflation is contrary to the interests of all Canadians, and that containment and reduction of inflation have become a matter of serious national concern. I say to the House that this sort of preamble has been treated in the courts as not justifying emergency action whereby the normal rights of the provinces are disregarded and set aside.
If the government really thought this was an emergency or anything like that, why did it not say so instead of using this language? I do not know whether it is ignorance, indifference, or contempt for the constitution-probably all three of them rolled into one.
I do not think it is a joke when parliament is invited by the government to evade the division of powers contained in sections 91 and 92 of the BNA Act, and then is told that some official in the Department of Justice says, "It is all right; we do not want you to bother about it." So much for the constitution, but I prophesy that this issue will rise up to smite the government eventually, probably after a long period of confusion.
Certainly if any client came to me very upset about the application of some of the powers under the act and wanted to go to the courts, I would be bound to tell him that I thought he had a real chance of winning the case and disrupting the whole administration of the act.
I want to deal with one other reason why I think this bill is most unsatisfactory and should not be accepted. I believe that it will provide for absolutely chaotic administration. What do we have? We have a whole series of boards under this bill. For example, the Anti-Inflation Board is not given the power to do anything very much except to monitor, to report, and to refer. It does not seem to want to confine itself to that. Certainly it has been issuing edicts, as it were, the authority for which is extremely dubious.
If we look at clause 12 of the bill we find little in there that gives any real power to the Anti-Inflation Board other than to make inquiries, monitor changes, and so on. After that inquiry has been gone through by the Anti-Inflation Board, we come to the administrator who is given full
Royal Assent
authority to enforce the act. However, he can only act when the Anti-Inflation Board or the governor in council advises him that there are reasonable grounds for believing that a supplier has contravened, or is likely to contravene the guidelines. Then the administrator has to make all the necessary inquiries and carry out hearings to determine what action, if any, could be taken. When he is through, there is an appeal to the Anti-Inflation Appeal Tribunal, and as if that were not enough, there is a further appeal to the federal court of appeal, a hierarchy of appeals which will lead to delay, confusion and, I prophesy, absolute chaos in the administration of this legislation.
We have heard enough about it already to know that chaos and confusion are growing. People are puzzled, to put it mildly, about the complexity of the guidelines. We do not know what legislation we are really passing, but we do know that almost absolute powers are conveyed to the governor in council, and that the government has not seen fit to refer the constitutionality of the legislation to the courts; and we know that on the face of it the administration, as I said, is likely to be chaotic.
For these reasons, as well as many others about the inequity and unfairness of this piece of legislation, I must declare myself to be against the bill. It is so framed as to invite the abdication of parliament, an invitation which of course will be accepted on the government side. No attempt has been made by the government to deal with the constitutional difficulties, and a chaotic administration is in prospect. For these reasons I think the right thing for us to do is to throw this bill out.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is in the process of trying to get Bill C-73 through third reading. I cannot say that I wish the government well or good luck with it. As we have said before, and I repeat again tonight, the bill is unfair, inequitable, and unjust. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has heard the words so often they must haunt him at night. I hope they do.
I look at this as not only an economic War Measures Act but as a sort Of ledger. On the debit side of the ledger are those who will be hurt most by this program. That is the majority of people in Canada. They are the ones who will be affected and the ones who will be ignored.
On the debit side of the ledger will be the pensioners and others on fixed income. Several times government spokesmen have said that the escalator will look after them. It will not. Even if it did, the basic pension is still insufficient.
On the debit side there are also those on minimum wages. Already one provincial government has tried to chisel, in the name of following the government's guidelines, on how much of an increase there is going to be in the minimum wage. Then there are the unorganized workers. At least two thirds, or 70 per cent, of the work force in Canada do not belong to a union. They do not have anyone to bargain for them. The government says that they can stay within the guidelines and get an increase of 10 per cent. This could be $600. If they happen to be highly paid, unorganized workers, they could get $2,400. I have not heard the government say that the Anti-Inflation Board will order employers of unorganized workers to guarantee them the $600. What they get will be that, or somewhat less.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner (London East)).)
The Anti-Inflation Board and the government's guidelines will discriminate against wage and salary earners, including unorganized workers and those who have been on a contract for the past one, two, or three years and are now negotiating a new one. These people have fallen behind. The board will only go through the motions of examining their case.
On the debit side of the ledger we find some 75 per cent or 80 per cent of the population who will be asked to carry the burden of this program on their shoulders.
On the credit side, we in our party, and I take it now those in the official opposition are waiting to hear what the government intends to do regarding profits, professional fees, and interest rates, measures which will affect those who are in the higher income brackets and represent only about 20 per cent of the population. But we have yet to hear anything from the government to illustrate that it can and will devise means to impose restraint on the people who occupy the credit side of the ledger. It has presented nothing to the House to illustrate the way in which it intends to enforce controls on the people who really cause inflation.
I listened with a feeling of nausea to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others in the government complaining about people who insist on extracting more from the economy than they put into it. I should like anyone in this chamber to tell me or anyone else that a person who is on the minimum wage is taking more out of the economy than he is putting into it. Are we really expected to believe that such people as these are causing inflation? If the government was genuine about this program it would take steps immediately to raise the minimum wage to $3.50 an hour and would be asking the provinces to do the same.
The people on minimum wages are not the ones who cause inflation; I am sure the Minister of Finance would not suggest that they are for one minute. People in receipt of pensions are not the ones who cause inflation People earning wages or salaries of less than $12,000 a year are not the ones who cause inflation.
When will the government learn that if you are going to fight inflation you must begin with the ones who cause inflation? You start at the top. You start with the high salaries, you start with dividends and professional fees which flow to the 20 per cent of the population who not only possess economic powers but seem to exercise political power altogether out of proportion to their numbers.
I would be one of the first to support a government of any political stripe in a fight against inflation if it attacked those who do in fact cause inflation. I cannot countenance a program which instead attacks only those who have no part in the cause of inflation, those who are its first victims, that is to say, people on low v/ages, pensioners, the majority of our citizens. I question the sincerity of a government which brings in a guidelines program requiring people who are on the lowest income scales to be in the forefront of the battle against inflation, to be the ones who man the barricades and go over the top in the charge against the spiral of rising prices.
What about the privileged, those w; derive the benefit of dividends, high interest rates, corporate profits and
December 2, 1975

professional fees? They are encouraging the government to do something about inflation. Of course the government brings in a program which does not particularly affect those who cause inflation.
Various voices were raised reminding the government that these are difficult times, that there was a rapid increase in the price of many products. Double-digit inflation, and so forth, led to demands that the government should do something about the situation-that it should take control over the economy, intervene in the economic field, and so on. I find this very interesting because, by and large, almost without exception those who have been most vocal and persistent in demanding that the government step in and impose controls are those who traditionally have been opposed to government intervention, namely, the business people, the free enterprisers, the capitalists.
Judging by press reports of the Prime Minister's speech in Assiniboia, Saskatchewan, the controls now being introduced by the government have been well received by the farmers, people who are often said to be the most independent in the country. I shall have more to say about that aspect in a few minutes.
What I find interesting is the fact that controls should have been advocated by the Conservatives and are being imposed by the Liberals, the two free-enterprise parties which have traditionally warned Canadians not to vote for the New Democratic Party because the NDP-ers would impose socialist controls. Mr. Speaker, if these controls resembled socialist controls there would be little or no work for me or anybody else in our group. Nevertheless, they are controls, and here are the free enterprise parties imposing them after screaming about socialists threatening to do so. One of those parties came out in 1974 in favour of a price freeze and certain controls. The other party said such a program would not work, that it couldn't be done. Now, in December, 1975, we find the Liberals and Conservatives have both made a 180 degree turn. I suppose that is to avoid a collision in the middle of the road.
I have a great deal of respect and regard for the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). He is one who has been consistent, honest, and straightforward. In fact I would be more comfortable living under some kind of control and restraint program if he were the prime minister. But he failed to make it. The fellow who told the Canadian people that controls would not work and couldn't be put into effect is the fellow who is now Prime Minister and pushing this bill through parliament.
As the premier of British Columbia said, these free enterprise parties get me all mixed up. These are the ones who said, "Don't vote for the NDP because they will bring in socialist controls; they will intervene in the sphere of private enterprise." Yet who are the ones who are demanding controls today-the Liberals and Conservatives!

While the government is instituting controls, the Liberals keep saying that they do not like controls but they see no other way out of present difficulties. They have both said they do not believe in them, that they do not like them, that they do not want them. What does the government do to curb these rising expectations? The government suggests to the people that they should not listen to the commercials and that they should not want those good things that are being advertised. I agree with the Prime Minister that we need a basic change in attitude in order to solve our economic problems. The whole exercise is futile in my opinion if we continue on our present course, because the inflation the Prime Minister complains about is promoted and advertised, all of which encourages these rising expectations which the Prime Minister claims ought to be dampened in order to fight inflation.
Let me say something about another aspect of this bill, and that is the so-called exemption for farmers and fishermen at the farm gate and at the dock. This is a charade and a window dressing. This is as phony as a $3 bill. It was bad enough to hear the Liberals say that the Conservative exemption for farmers at the farm gate in 1974 was phony, but to see the Liberal government proving itself to be phony is something else again. It is even worse.
I have a document here which I am sure many other members have now, although it is marked confidential. It was issued by the Department of Finance on November 17, 1975. The minister's own officials put in writing how phony this protection at the farm gate and at the dock is. In the first paragraph the minister's officials say in this confidential document, and you can imagine how confidential it is if I have one:
Farmers and fishermen are exempt from the guidelines, since, as a rule, they are unorganized and have little power in the market.
That is not what Ma Plumptre says about the egg marketing board. According to the officials of the Minister of Finance they have little power in the market. The document goes on to state:
-the federal government wants to ensure that they operate within the spirit of the anti-inflation program.
When I turn over two pages of this interesting little document from the minister's officials I find illustrated four kinds of marketing boards that are apparently to be subject to the application of the guidelines. These kinds of marketing boards, or two of them, are concerned with the handling of chicken broilers, turkeys, eggs, industrial milk, fresh fruits and fresh vegetables, as well as hogs, potatoes, soybeans, corn, tobacco, and fruits and vegetables for processing. This is what the minister's officials say about these marketing boards:

These boards will have to be reviewed before reaching firm decisions on which ones should be subject to the guidelines and which of their costs should be allowable under the cost-pass-through rule.
The first page of this document says they are exempt from the guidelines, and the third page outlines which ones "should be subject to the guidelines".
In respect of the cost-pass-through rule the Minister of Finance attempted to answer a question I asked in the House the other day, yet the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board had already eliminated three costs of production under the grain stabilization bill.
My friends in the official opposition have talked about this exemption at the farm gate for the farmers and at the docks for the fishermen. I would ask them how they feel now about this program that was to exempt the farmers and fishermen when in fact statements of those leaders of the Anti-Inflation Board, Pepin and Plumptre, and statements in writing by officials of the Minister of Finance, have proven that this is a farce. It is as phony as a $3 bill. Marketing boards will in fact be subject to the guidelines and will be treated the same as wage and salary earners.
The farmers and the fishermen, whether or not they belong to a marketing board or agency that can set or negotiate prices for them, will have to appear and prove to the Anti-Inflation Board that the increase is justified. All this talk about exempting the farmers and the fishermen has gone out the window. I suggest it was out the window the day after the Prime Minister presented this program to the people of Canada.
I am not going to support any program such as this which attacks the wage and salary earners and those people on fixed incomes. I do not intend to support a program which makes liars of the government members. I am not going to be a party to a program that helps make liars of the Liberal government, or helps the members of that government make liars of themselves. Obviously this is the case because they say the farmers and fishermen are exempt, and then in this written document outline which of these marketing boards shall be subject to the guidelines.

Most provinces have marketing boards in respect of broilers, turkeys, eggs, hogs, milk, fresh vegetables and fruit crops. Since there are import controls on eggs and turkeys the national agencies can theoretically set prices arbitrarily. In practice the egg marketing agency until very recently had great difficulty in maintaining a price that would adequately cover the cost of production. In fact the Farm Products Marketing Council wants officials of CEMA to appear monthly in order to justify the price it sets for eggs.
These agencies have always been under guidelines and controls. Ma Plumptre and Jean-Luc Pepin say that the first outfits they want to look into are the marketing boards, specifically CEMA. How long can any government exercise control over wages and salaries and not food prices? What is the government going to do about marketing boards? What about the price of milk; what about the price of bread? I say as a warning to my friends in the official opposition that the longer and the more strictly wages and salaries are controlled, the more insistent the demand will become for stringent controls on food prices. I cannot see any government of any political stripe ingoring those demands.
If the farmers and the businessmen think wages have gone out of sight, let us look at food prices. The prices the farmers are getting are prices they should have been getting years ago. They have been the victims of a cheap food policy in this country for decades. We have lost 300,000 family farm units in this country since the Second World War. Again I will use Manitoba as an example for the benefit of my hon. friend from Provencher.
The average industrial wage in Manitoba from 1972 to 1975 increased by 30 per cent. The price of eggs went up 50 per cent, turkeys 37 per cent, broiler chickens 80 per cent, shoulder roasts 181 per cent, pork chops 63 per cent, and bacon 158 per cent. Is my hon. friend from Provencher, or anyone else in the official opposition, going to say that wages are too high in the face of the food increases? This situation exists in every province in Canada. The price of sirloin steak and prime rib roast went up by 73 per cent and 44 per cent respectively, while industrial wages rose by 30 per cent. As a representative of several thousand farmers and people who live on farms I say it is easy to see why the consumers are becoming upset and downright angry when their wages are to be controlled and the price of food is to be left free.
What has happened? Under this legislation we have the same old dividing game. We have the farmers and workers with controlled wages and salaries and farm prices. The farmers are told they are exempt, but under the way in which they are subject to the guidelines, the marketing boards that they have fought for over decades are in jeopardy and are being investigated while those who

cause inflation, the people who benefit from the difference in price between what the farmers receive and the cost of the products to consumers, are not controlled. I refer to the processors, the transporters, the wholesalers, and the retailers. The controls are not spelled out for these people. They can take all they can get.
The primary producer and the wage and salary earners are being told, and in fact required under this legislation, to fight inflation. Those who may profit whether because of interest rates, corporate profits, dividends, or professional fees can get around the controls. I will not be a party to the support of legislation of this kind. The members of the official opposition have all caved in. I would like to know why they have chickened out.
Earlier the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) talked a good fight, but now they have all caved in. It is no wonder the voters of Canada chose not to put them in power. I hope my hon. friends to the right will get up and take a further part in this debate. However, I suppose they will just sit there. If my time has expired I hope my friends will say I can have some more time. I am very serious about this.
I want members of the official opposition to stand up and help us fight this legislation. I would be interested in hearing their explanation of how they would exempt farm products at the farm gate. I would also be interested in hearing how they would control profits, interest rates, and prices. It might be helpful if the government would reject this legislation and take it back to the drafting board. Obviously the officials wrote it out on the back of an envelope before Thanksgiving. I make no apology if some government members should accuse me of being unpatriotic, but I will encourage all the people in my area not to co-operate in respect of this legislation because it is unfair.

speechtext:
I have already mentioned housing. The government could deal with that, but it would have to take tough action with the banks, so we are not going to have anything but the fiddling around which the Minister of State for Urban Affairs is going to be doing in the next few weeks with regard to housing. We will not get the capital we need going into housing. The government will not deal with the banks or the petroleum industry, so we have inflation in those sectors and will continue to have inflation regardless of this bill. When the vote comes, as it will come, there will be no effect on those sectors because the government has no program to increase supply.
In some speeches back in the 1974 election campaign the Prime Minister used to talk about increasing supply. That was when the Liberals at least had some kind of intellectual consistency. They recognized that the way to deal with inflation, then as now, was to take major steps to increase supply. However, perhaps they recognize that to do so would entail getting tough with their corporate friends, and they refuse to take the appropriate steps. Instead they have singled out the wage and salary earner as the person who is to bear the burden of this program, and I do not know anyone who has argued against that. There is no question that the wage and salary earner will be affected.
What the government said when it brought in the program in its white paper was that it recognized certain injustices would automatically follow if everyone were bound by the 10 per cent to 12 per cent guideline, so the government agreed to recognize historical relationships. I refer the backbenchers of the Liberal Party to page 31 of the white paper. There the exceptions are listed, and in the white paper the government says that if a historical relationship between two groups can be established and that if the group now bargaining, depending on the dates of its contract expiring, and so on, can establish a case, then the phrase used will be that the wage settlement or salary settlement proposed, and recommended by the anti-inflation board, will be to maintain the historical relationship.
The decision handed down by the Anti-Inflation Board last Friday completely contradicted the white paper. The Minister of Finance refused to answer a question on it in the House today, but that is exactly what it did. The Anti-Inflation Board said that it recognized the historical relationship which exists between elementary and secondary school teachers in Toronto. The fact is that for the past 21 years the two groups have had the same salaries. I assume the Liberals can read. To implement the white paper, which they are responsible for writing, the AntiInflation Board should at least as a minimum have said that the high school teachers in Toronto were entitled to
December 2, 1975

the benefits and the salaries the elementary school teachers received.
However, what did the board do? The board said it recognized the relationship, but that the teachers are not going to get the money. What this amounts to is a flat contradiction of the white paper, and I am glad to see that some Liberals are nodding their heads in agreement. I hope they make a speech on that point.
