subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
This program is wrong because it is unfair and unworkable for reasons I, and other members of my party, have documented since the bill was first introduced. It is wrong in terms of its own detail, but more important, in terms of the national problem of inflation. It is wrong because it does not address itself in a positive way to bringing forth programs which would deal with housing prices, energy prices, and food prices. It is in these three sectors where inflation has occurred in Canada, and there has been no debate in the House in that regard.
I find it extraordinary that for the whole period of time we have discussed Bill C-73 there has been nothing from the government side to the effect that in the last three years 65 per cent of our inflation has occurred in housing, food costs, and energy. I have not heard hon. members opposite tell us what the government would like to do with regard to those three items. Instead the government brought in a program which is primary in its effects, and every economist says that. It is going to be solely aimed at wage and salary earners. One might say that perhaps wage and salary earners are the problem.
If anything could justify the government's 180 degree about turn since July, 1974, it would be to be able to establish its case that wage and salary increases now are the main culprits in terms of inflation. The fact is that statistics have not been brought forward. The government has produced no evidence to show that wage and salary increases are the cause of inflation. I say it has not because it knows it cannot bring out the evidence. It does not exist.
Anti-Inflation Act
If you look at the OECD reports or the figures issued by Statistics Canada, wage and salary increases have been running behind the increases in the cost of living. The governor of the Bank of Canada and others have said that, but the minister does not attempt to deal with the argument.
On the other hand in terms of our trade position, that other whipping boy of the government, it says we will price ourselves out of world markets. The evidence does not support the government's case that when compared with other trading nations we are pricing ourselves out of world markets. Our major trading partners have wage and salary increases exceeding those in Canada.
The government cannot justify its program. It bears directly on wage and salary earners, but the evidence in Canada is that wage and salary earners in this country are not having increases disproportionate to those of other trading countries. In terms of domestic inflation, wage and salary earners have been following the increases in the cost of living, principally in food, housing, and energy. They have not caused the increase.
The government brought its program to the people of Canada and I suggest the reason was that just before Thanksgiving Day the former minister of finance decided to pack it all in. God knows his reasons, and I am not going to speculate on them. The people of Canada have been asking for leadership. They have said, "Where is this man who was elected in July, 1974, who said that only the Liberals would provide the leadership?" Even the Liberals, with a majority, began to sense that 99 per cent of the people of Canada were unhappy. It finally got through- from July, 1974, to September, 1975. So the Prime Minister said, "We had better do something. Turner has packed it in and the people are unhappy, so we had better come through with a symbolic act. We cannot do a War Measures Act again because the people of Quebec are not causing the trouble they were five years ago." Even though that was a grotesque injustice then, it had a symbolic flair. So he brought out a program that will not affect corporate decision-making in this country one iota.
He wants the American economy to bail us out. It will take off in the next 12 months and we will get the spin-off effects in employment and inflation. He said, "Let's hook up to a program that will not affect corporate decisionmaking but will bear directly on wage and salary earners." He made a symbolic appearance on television telling the people it is time to make sacrifices. He thought it really looked as if it had substance to it. In my judgment it is a hoax of a program; it is entirely a political gesture, and apart from the control of wages and salaries it has no economic substance at all. Once again the Liberal party is gambling on the Americans to bail us out.
I want to conclude with one further observation, Mr. Speaker. The major organized opponents of this legislation outside the House of Commons have been the trade union movement. In my view they have been absolutely right in their perspective. The program exempts corporations from any effective control of their prices, and consumers all across the country know this. The unions have been right in saying this. In my opinion they have also been right in

December 2, 1975

Anti-Inflation Act
pointing out that they were not going to be the principal people to suffer. They are going to get their 10 per cent or 12 per cent but, Mr. Speaker, they comprise only 35 per cent of the workers in Canada.

To their immense credit-and to the disgrace of the press-the trade union movement has singled out the non-trade union workers in this country as being the people who will suffer most. This is what we have been saying too.
The government knows that a report came out last week which shows that 50 per cent of Canadians on pensions live in poverty. Mr. Speaker, 50 per cent of the people in this affluent society who live on pensions live in poverty, and 22 per cent of Canadians in general live in poverty.
The government did nothing about increasing the federal minimum wage. It did nothing about encouraging the provinces to increase their minimum wage.

Mr. Speaker, it is too bad that Hansard cannot record a yawn from Liberal backbenchers. I got the biggest sigh from a Liberal backbencher when I mentioned that most Canadians live in poverty. He knows that the government has a cabinet which is the highest paid in the world. I do not know how many Canadians know that. The Canadian cabinet is the highest paid in the world and its members just gave themselves a very substantial increase. I have not checked this yet, but my guess is that the top 5 per cent of Canadian civil servants are probably the highest paid in the world as well. I have not checked that, but I suspect it is true.
We have a nice little contented elite running this country. It operates on the one hand through the corporate sector and on the other hand through the Liberal Party of Canada. They are so insulated from reality that they can bring in a program like this and have the audacity to say that low income earners in our country can get $600-they raised that. You can now earn $7,500 per year and they will not object. They know full well that there is absolutely no way for unorganized workers in Canada to get that increase.
The Liberals have done nothing for the vast majority of Canadian men and women not in the trade union movement, have done nothing for the pensioners half of whom live in poverty, but have done everything by means of providing loopholes for the corporations, whether they be banks, real estate speculators, food chains, you name it. This is a classic piece of legislation; it favours those who have against those who have not. It is precisely for that reason that we oppose it.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a very important piece of legislation facing the Canadian people. I have listened with interest to the comments made by the official opposition during the time the bill has been before us, and I have been interested in the comments by Liberal backbenchers at second reading and report stage.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: All two of them.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The comments indicate the weaknesses and the inequities in this legislation as demonstrated by the fact that we are seeing a great deal of trouble developing in a large segment of the population. They were surprised at the difficulties the bill had created. That sums it up fairly well.
A large segment of the population is violently opposed to this bill. Very few think that it will do anything for them. Those I have talked to are either neutral or violently opposed to it. I have not found any in favour of it.
I have read the conclusions in the white paper. It may be a good idea to put two paragraphs on the record so that hon. members, particularly those on the government side, can decide whether this debate is accomplishing any of the aims stated in the conclusions in the white paper. If we have not accomplished all or a large percentage of them, we have failed the Canadian public.
It is true that almost all Canadians welcomed the statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on Thanksgiving Day. They did so for one reason. He had finally decided to do something about the problem. Everyone is concerned about inflation. Therefore when the Prime Minister said that something would be done about it, good, bad or indifferent, most Canadians were interested.
Since that time Canadians have been listening to radio, watching television, and reading newspaper reports. They have not heard of the Prime Minister explaining any aspects of the bill in this House. However, he has travelled across the country explaining it. He failed in almost every area, even where the audience was loaded, to convince them that he had come anywhere near reaching the aims set out in the conclusions of the White Paper on inflation. Some of those conclusions are worth considering on third reading. I quote from the conclusion in "Attack on Inflation, a Program of National Action":
As a first essential, it is imperative that we take determined action as a nation to halt and reverse the spiral of costs and prices that jeopardizes the whole fabric of our economy and of our society.
I am sure almost everyone agrees with that. Only a few were of the opinion that we should allow spiralling costs to go unchecked, something that is detrimental to our economy. The reason they were opposed is that they were on a treadmill. Everyone was looking for more income, no matter what sources, because they were having one hell of a time keeping up with the cost of living; society was affected because it had become disproportionate.
As the leader of the New Democratic Party just stated, the poor were becoming poorer. A large percentage were below the poverty line and in no position to do anything about it. I think everyone will agree that the aim in the conclusion was good. However, they will now have to be convinced that we have done something to solve the problem of spiralling prices. We have done something to curtail the ability of a large segment of the population to cope with spiralling costs. While income has been pegged at 10 per cent, the cost of living increase is estimated at 13 per cent. No matter how you look at it, everyone will be going backwards. If you carry this far enough, we will be reaching the point where everyone will be below the poverty

December 2, 1975

level except those with income other than wages or salaries.
I again refer to the conclusions in the white paper. This bothers me. Obviously it must be the aim of the Prime Minister because this is what he talked about on Thanksgiving evening. I quote:
This will require the exercise of restraint by every sector and the pursuit of fiscal and monetary policies aimed at ensuring sustained and stable economic growth. Over the longer term we must make our economic system more innovative, dynamic and efficient by reducing existing rigidities and intensifying competition.
That has not been done. Anyone with a new idea, anyone who wants competition or wants to improve their position will be curtailed. That does not apply to companies or those connected with the price structure. It only applies to those receiving wages and salaries. It goes on, and I quote:
We must deal with major structural problems so as to ensure an adequate supply of energy, food and housing to meet our needs in the years ahead. And finally we must ensure that sufficient physical and financial resources will become available to complete the massive new capital investment that is required over the next decade and more, to increase substantially our productive capacity, employment and our real standard of living.
This bill does not go anywhere near accomplishing that aim. The government is not embarking on any new programs to provide future employment. In fact it is going to curtail some necessary expenditures such as those related to health. The Conservative party, on the other hand, wants to go much further and curtail almost all government expenditures.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) pointed out that one province does not have much left after meeting the basic needs of the community. If there is to be any curtailing it will have to be of services provided to those not able to provide for themselves.
There is not one clause in this bill that gives any indication of increased productivity or increased employment. More taxes will be required, not less. Government expenditures will be greater because more people will be unemployed than ever before. If what we want is more unemployment, we are going about it the right way. Money has not been spent in the Department of Labour although four or five competent people are required to learn the art of negotiation in order that industry in this country can be provided with some assistance in connection with negotiations. Mr. Speaker, you must laugh as you look around the House to hear the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) answering questions when he is asked what help he is providing to get a resumption of work in the pulp and paper industry.
We are not interested in the constitution as far as the bill before us is concerned. We have probably broken through every possible constitutional barrier. My hon. friend from Greenwood told us tonight he would be quite prepared to take almost any section of this legislation before the Supreme Court and challenge it on constitutional grounds. Yet the Minister of Labour stands up and says he can do nothing about the situation in the pulp and paper industry because it is a provincial matter. It makes no difference that in the bill before us we are asked to give the government power to make decisions which will create serious unemployment in provincial fields.
Anti-Inflation Act
We are going to see a great deal of unemployment in the educational field, as well as in the civil service in the Province of Ontario, despite the fact the federal government has no jurisdiction, except by permission, over matters affecting education or the public service in Ontario.
I quote again:
Governments at all levels in Canada can and must provide leadership and direction but they cannot act alone. All sectors of the economy must actively co-operate. This requires the fullest possible discussion and consultation as to how best to achieve our mutual goals.
There is no one in this country who does not agree that this is essential. Yet what co-operation do we find in this House? I am not suggesting that all the wisdom of the country is gathered in this place. Nevertheless I do say that a number of the concrete proposals made to the government in the past few weeks might have been adopted. I was not one who sat on the committee which considered this matter, but I am sure many suggestions were put forward which, had they been adopted, would have made co-operation possible and would have led to more acceptable legislation. As things stand, the bill will likely be passed only after a division; the majority of members on the government side will, no doubt, support it, and the majority of members in the opposition will likely oppose it.
What is the basis for Bill C-73? It is based on the white paper, and the conclusion reached by that white paper was in these terms:
The attack on inflation ... was designed to ensure that the recovery of our economy from its present recession leads to healthy and enduring growth in employment and real incomes. These basic objectives are shared by business, labour, governments and indeed by all Canadians. We all have a compelling interest to work together.
There is no one who will disagree with that conclusion either. If we are to be fair, if we are to be reasonable, if we are to act in the interest of the Canadian people, we must provide leadership on two fronts simultaneously: we shall have to reduce the rate at which the cost of living is rising, and, second, we shall have to curtail the rise in unemployment. The bill before us does neither, and if it fails to achieve either of these objectives it seems to me it is not worthy of support and that it will not be supported by the Canadian people.
Where does this show up? It shows up in the reaction of the organized labour movement which has always been proud of the fact that it can look after itself in a free enterprise system. The organized labour movement in Canada is built on the basis of the free enterprise system. It has always been willing to operate within that system. It has done very well, in my opinion, for its membership. Nevertheless a large section of the population is not organized. I refer to those who live on old age pensions, disability pensions, pensions under the Canada Pension Plan and so on. Their incomes must be brought up to a reasonable standard if this legislation is to succeed. Yet nothing has been done in this direction. On the contrary, we heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) proposing to cut off a portion of the assistance made available to the provinces to help these underprivileged persons.
People are asking how they are to know that prices are being curtailed. Not long ago I heard a minister being

December 2, 1975
Adjournment Debate
asked about the price of carrots, whether the price of carrots would be controlled every day. I agree it is not possible to control the price of carrots on a day-to-day basis. If the amount held in storage diminishes, or if it is necessary to import the product from abroad, the price would probably have to go up anyway. But if the price goes up, there has to be some justification for it. The government has said to the householder, "Your wages are to be controlled." But it has failed to assure the housewife that the prices of the products she needs are not going to rise. That is where the bill is defective.
I should like to show the House how little the farmer gets from the commodities the housewife uses, products which are so important to her, and, incidentally, how little the retailer gets out of them. But what a hosing the Canadian people get from the wholesaler, the packers, and the other trades in the middle-people like Kraft who have a monopoly over a large segment of the producing industry. May I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: STORMS-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO THOSE SUFFERING DAMAGE IN LAKE ERIE REGION
STORMS-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO THOSE SUFFERING DAMAGE IN LAKE ERIE REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising this evening is to follow up a question I put to the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve) on November 17 as reported in Hansard at page 9106. It concerned storm damage on the north of Lake Erie. It reads as follows:
I should like to ask the minister whether the government has taken any initiative in approaching the province of Ontario, which is assessing the damage, with a view to declaring the north shore a disaster area in order that individuals, communities and small businesses which have suffered grievous losses will qualify for federal assistance.
The minister replied rather briefly as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the department has not taken the initiative because that initiative should come from the government of the province of Ontario.
In view of the extent of the damage I thought this was rather a brush-off and I wanted more information; hence my appearance here tonight.
It was early in November that a storm of hurricane proportions struck the area, the like of which has seldom been seen before. As a result of wave action, of proportions not seen before either, property damage was sustained. It is a shallow lake and huge waves were hurled against the shoreline. Erosion of farmland occurred as well as destruction of cottages, some of which were a write-off. Break-walls and breakwaters were washed away. Cemeteries along the shoreline were eroded until the graves themselves were exposed. Roads were washed out and pavement peeled off as one would peel the skin from a potato.
The high water driven up on to the shore by the force of the wind caused a rise of some four to five feet in the waterline, something never before seen. This of course caused flooding along the shoreline, cottages were flooded as well as even permanent homes. Rugs, furniture and so on were damaged, some beyond repair. Marinas were damaged, fishing tugs were lost, and one man's life was lost through this raging storm.
I later contacted the clerks and/or mayors of each municipality in my riding, which has property along the north shore of Lake Erie, to get an estimate from them of the loss sustained during the storm. This was a week or two later when they had had an opportunity to assess the damage. The town of Dunnville felt that the damage would be in excess of $75,000; the town of Haldimand $236,700; the city of Nanticoke $200,000; the township of Delhi $42,000; the township of Norfolk $100,000. This made a total of $653,000. In addition to that, and since I asked my question, there was another violent storm, though not of the same proportions, and the damage increased again. I now estimate the total damage is in the neighbourhood of $800,000.
This of course has pushed the total damage up to an amount that cannot easily be borne by the individuals concerned and/or the communities in the area. My question referred to the possibility of declaring the north shore a disaster area so that the province and the federal government would alike share the assistance provided to these people.
Since that time I do not think I would go so far as to ask that it be declared a disaster area, even though the damage
December 2, 1975

is extensive, as I have indicated. However, the losses are of such magnitude as to place an undue financial burden on individuals, municipalities, and small businesses, particularly the fishing industry in the area. I talked with the hon. Mr. Bernier, the minister of the environment for the province of Ontario, and his department conducted an aerial survey of the north shore and affirmed that the damage was not quite as extensive as at first thought. The province indicated that it is willing to give some assistance in the form of loans.
What I want to know from the Minister of the Environment or the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), who I am pleased to see in the House tonight to answer my representation, is in what specific ways the government can assist municipalities or individuals who have suffered. I know he is going to say that in such cases we share alike with the province of Ontario, or whatever is the province involved, but I want to know whether there are any other ways that the federal government can directly help these people. I wonder whether there is any means under ARDA whereby the federal government can assist in this situation. After all, there has been terrific loss of farm land due to the erosive effect of waves along the north shore of Lake Erie.
I should like to refer to one farm at Port Burwell, in one corner of my riding, owned by a Mr. Balther, where not due to this one storm but over a period of years one third of his farm land has been lost. I want to know what it is the federal government is prepared to do to assist people who find themselves in this situation. That is the question I am asking tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Baker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment and Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: STORMS-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO THOSE SUFFERING DAMAGE IN LAKE ERIE REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can certainly sympathize with the hon. gentleman, coming from a province in which we have disasters quite frequently amounting to the approximate magnitude about which the hon. member was speaking.
The Federal Disaster Assistance Program, as the House is probably aware, is administered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). While the program is not embodied in legislation, it provides for discretionary payments by the federal government to assist the provinces in the event of disasters. Such payments are made only when the provincial expenditure eligible for sharing exceeds $1 per capita and, of course, only after the province has made a request for such assistance. So it would be something like $8 million for the province of Ontario. Unfortunately, eligible costs do not include summer cottages.
In the case of the Lake Erie storm on November 10, 1975, to which the hon. gentleman referred, damages to structures according to our department were in the order of $500,000 but, as the hon. gentleman has pointed out, this has risen to $653,000 and, as he suggests, perhaps goes up to $800,000. The damages were mainly to cottages, some permanent residences, and some private protective structural devices. The hon. member has already elaborated on other things that were damaged. In addition, there was considerable damage in the form of erosion.
As hon. members can appreciate, this falls below the minimum of $1 per capita for Ontario. No request has been
Adjournment Debate
received from the government of that province for assistance, obviously because of the formula that is used.
The hon. member asked about other means by which the people affected can get assistance. I obtained this information from the department today and it is something I did not know about previously, though I wish I had known.
The province of Ontario has its own policies in this regard, and there is also the Canadian Disaster Relief Fund which administers funds left over from the Winnipeg flood of the 1950's. I understand that in case of individual relief, payments can be made up to 50 per cent of the family's losses, to a maximum of $2,250 per family. Application for assistance from the fund is usually made, as I am told, by the province after assessment and consolidation of individual claims.
That appears to be the only recourse the hon. gentleman has, and I appreciate his deep concern for the people in that area.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL STUDY OF ANOTHER TRANSPORTATION LINK BETWEEN NEW BRUNSWICK AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-GOVERNMENT ACTION
TRANSPORT-FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL STUDY OF ANOTHER TRANSPORTATION LINK BETWEEN NEW BRUNSWICK AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I again wish to raise a question I put to the then minister of transport on July 16 regarding the report of a joint federal-provincial task force concerning another transportation link between New Brunswick and the western part of Prince Edward Island.
This is one of a series of studies that has been received recently. The then minister of transport of course is now the Minister without Portfolio, and we have a new minister who I hope in his zeal to fulfil many of the needs for a transportation policy across Canada will look very seriously at this particular continuing study. Indeed, reviewing the amount of study that has taken place on this subject over the past 30 years, if all studies were laid end to end this would likely be sufficient to bridge the gap between western Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
I think it would be acknowledged by all members that there is a basic federal responsibility to ensure a most adequate and up-to-date means of transportation between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
It is obvious to me as well that there are a number of benefits that would be gained from the establishment of a further ferry link to the western end of Prince Edward Island. One of those was pointed out very clearly in a study done some 12 years ago by the Maritime Transport Commission, in which it is stated:
It is therefore clear that the underlying factor supporting the proposed service is the "pioneering" or developmental effect it would have on the economy of the W. Prince area.
I think that is still true today. One of the unfortunate facts that exists at the moment is that one of the reports upon which the government may be basing some of its conclusions is a report that seemed to omit almost entirely that particular aspect which I regard as basic. This is the report of the ADI Consultant Group from Fredericton as presented to the minister in June of this year, which supports the call by the West Prince Chamber of Commerce for an independent study. It is no doubt clear that

there are some basic and fundamental studies in respect of Prince Edward Island transportation.
An official connected with provincial and federal parks in Prince Edward Island noted that those in the central part of the province are on the verge of an irreversible deterioration in their physical, asthetic, and social environments as there is need for a very basic program of tourist diversion if the whole industry is not to suffocate. Given the desire of most tourists to go the circle route or to travel end to end in the province, a new ferry on the western end of Prince Edward Island is an integral if not an essential element of the provincial government's policy of balanced tourist development across all of Prince Edward Island. I believe as well that basic industries such as farming and fishing undoubtedly would benefit from the reduced shipping time which is so vital to their interests in terms of moving perishable products during the peak seasons.
Support for a new crossing has come from a variety of sources-the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, the Chambers of Commerce of Prince Edward Island, and in New Brunswick-the Atlantic Truckers Association as well as most recently the joint federal-provincial Kent County tourism study which was partially funded by the federal government, which said very clearly that the establishment of such ferry service would be extremely feasible.
I think the conclusion was also drawn that it would offer a great deal of benefit to the eastern region of the Kent County area of New Brunswick. This is an increasing development which I think indicates the degree with which we are looking at a transportation development not just for one province but ultimately for two.
Quite frankly, I said at the outset I was disturbed by the quality of one of the studies which is before us at the moment, the ADI study. I think if the federal government or the Department of Transport is relying on this study which has been released recently, which purports to do a cost-benefit analysis of a West Prince Kent County water crossing, I find this to be totally unsatisfactory as the report obviously is inadequate. It suffers from the lack of a very real consideration of the basic elements. In the first instance as much as I was able to determine there was actualy little or no consultation with people in the affected areas, those who stand most to gain or presently to lose by the absence of such a ferry service.
I think, too, the very questionable techniques used in forecasting traffic volume and in sufficiently understanding their potential indicate the superficial aspects of the ADI report. It is obvious that the establishment of new highway routes, especially those now under construction in New Brunswick, should have the effect of considerably improving the time-saving for motorists who are tourists and ultimately those who would be using the crossing to move produce to and from Prince Edward Island. There is an over-all lack of a comprehensive analysis of the effect of the new crossing on the tourist industry and on related factors of the economy.
I believe, as does the West Prince Chamber of Commerce, that there needs to be an independent assessment of this ADI study, and of course some of the previous studies. If we are to rely totally on the narrow and isolated base of

the ADI study the new crossing may well appear economically unjustified, but taken in the context of an over-all developmental strategy for Prince Edward Island, as it should, then the new crossing would probably represent a healthy net benefit. I think the same would be true in the development of Kent County.
This I believe is another example of a lack of coming to grips with some of the basic elements involved in a developmental policy. We have had many considerations and studies but much of this has been superficial. There is an obvious need for a commitment to a transportation program aimed at development. At the present time such seems to be virtually non-existent. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Goodale) can assure me there is a more comprehensive report now under way which will soon be presented which will recommend a program of action to establish this badly needed ferry link.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL STUDY OF ANOTHER TRANSPORTATION LINK BETWEEN NEW BRUNSWICK AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much indeed the comments of my hon. friend from Egmont. I appreciate the manner in which he delivered his remarks this evening on a subject which is important to the particular region of the country from which he comes.
I regret my inability this evening to offer a specific answer and to be able to tell him when precisely a more comprehensive report might be forthcoming on the situation which he described. I have before me now the report of which he was critical, that is the West Prince-Kent County ferry study which was jointly funded by the federal Ministry of Transport, the department of industry and commerce of the province of Prince Edward Island, and the department of economic growth in New Brunswick.
As the hon. member pointed out, one of the specific and unequivocal findings of that study was that there was little, if any, economic justification for the kind of ferry service which the hon. member and others no doubt are advocating in the circumstances which he described. The analysis in that report, looking at it in a quick way, is detailed, at least in appearance, but I appreciate the remarks which the hon. member addressed to the House this evening, pointing out what he, and no doubt others, regard as defects in the analysis. I am sure those comments will come to the attention of those who presently have this study under advisement, and I hope they will be guided to a reasonable extent by the remarks the hon. member made this evening.
This report is now a public document and has been made available to interested parties, and I hope others as well who have criticism of this study or any of the other studies will make them known to the minister so their views on the subject can go into the total decision making process. The findings and analysis of this specific study are presently being assessed in the context of the over-all requirements of P.E.I. and mainland transportation planning. Transport Canada is actively engaged in this comprehensive work, and I hope the hon. member will not have to wait an inordinate length of time before the Ministry of Transport will be able to give him a specific indication as to when the results of that over-all effort will be available publicly.

subtopic: NATIONAL FILM BOARD-PROPOSAL THAT OPEN COMPETITION WITH BOARD BE PERMITTED-GOVERNMENT POSITION
NATIONAL FILM BOARD-PROPOSAL THAT OPEN COMPETITION WITH BOARD BE PERMITTED-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 25 I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) whether he would consider an amendment to the National Film Board Act to delete sections 9 and 11 of that act. The National Film Board is now 30 years old, it is reaching a ripe maturity and, according to the 1974-75 annual report, has 950 employees on its staff. I must say that the statement on page 35 of that report is somewhat misleading. It reads:
In line with the board's policy to support the Canadian film industry, 50 per cent of the dollar volume of government department films and other audio visual materials was contracted out to the private sector.
That may be a very accurate statement as it stands, but the report does not say how much of that 50 per cent is given to audio visual production and how much is given to film production. My understanding is that less than 10 per cent of films for government departments are produced by firms in the private sector. The fact is that sections 9 and 11 stipulate that all contracts for film production for government departments first, must be approved by the Treasury department-that is an understandable regulation- and second, must be approved by the National Film Board. I submit that that is a blatant case of conflict of interest.
Who in the world could imagine anyone in the private sector submitting a tender for a contract if that tender had to be studied and approved by the competition? The immediate question has to be: how safe is any proposal if it can be refused by the National Film Board when it is submitted to the government department and, even more important, how may times have those ideas submitted by the private sector to the government been incorporated in the production of the National Film Board once they knew what that production was all about? The related question is: how objective can we expect the National Film Board to be with projects that are not its own responsibility? However, a corollary to that, I think, is the burden of my remarks tonight.
What is the minister afraid of? Are 30 years of monopoly of government business not enough to establish an industry in a sound competitive position? Are 950 people not enough to compete with the small producers? Is the minister afraid that a company of 10 or 12 people with three or four cameras will be unfair competition, or have an unfair advantage over the National Film Board, with capital equipment assets of over $4 million and unlimited distribution facilities? What is the minister afraid of? Is the problem that the National Film Board, after 30 years of practical monopoly of government business, is afraid to compete with the small, independent film producer?
The minister has said many times that he wants to help establish an independent film industry in Canada. I suggest that here is one great way he can help them. All these people want is the opportunity to compete fairly with the National Film Board for government filming contracts. Is that too much to ask? Ironically one such company has done more work for the United States government than for the Canadian government. Something is rotten in the state
Adjournment Debate
of Denmark, and when I asked the question originally the answer was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I have had these representations made to me by a variety of sources within the industry. I have promised to look into them, but I am not sure that this is the remedy.
I ask the minister, what is the remedy? If after 30 years in a monopoly situation the Film Board is not in a position yet to compete with small, independent producers, we must seriously question the competence of the National Film Board or the seriousness of the minister when he says that he wants to help establish an independent film industry in Canada.
I should like to have a direct answer from the minister or his parliamentary secretary as to what degree we can count on the seriousness of the minister when he says that he would like to support the private film industry, and what opportunities he will take to do that.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: NATIONAL FILM BOARD-PROPOSAL THAT OPEN COMPETITION WITH BOARD BE PERMITTED-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from its inception in 1939 the National Film Board of Canada was given a mandate to promote the production and distribution of films in the national interest. Section 9 states it is to represent the Government of Canada in its relations with persons engaged in commercial motion picture film activity in connection with motion picture films for the government or any department thereof.
This is a role which the National Film Board has carried out with such effect that it is now recognized around the world as a model which other countries emulate. Numbers of National Film Board productions, many of them made for government departments, have won national and international awards.
The board's success did not, however, prevent it from developing a program of contracting out an increasing volume of sponsored film business, from the point at which the film industry had developed its capability to handle it.
In July, 1972, the cabinet, as a part of the national film policy, recommended the establishment of a special committee on sponsored films. The committee, chaired by the Treasury Board, is looking specifically at the National Film Board mandate in relation to the production of film for government departments and agencies, and has received briefs from various private sector organizations. It is anticipated that the committee's report will be presented to the minister in the next two months. While we cannot speculate on the content of the report, the following information may be useful to the hon. member.
The National Film Board has reduced its own production activities in the sponsored film program over the past five fiscal years, in order to provide an increasing share to the private sector. This shift which has taken place in the private sector's share of sponsored film production is from 8 per cent in 1970-71 to 50 per cent in 1974-75.
It is also important to recognize that support to the private sector from the National Film Board is not limited to the sponsored film program, which in 1974-75 was worth $1.6 million to the private sector. In addition to the $1.6 million, the NFB spent a further $5 million in laboratories for processing, for prints, and other private sector creative and technical services. This support is part of the govern-
